items.description: «Άνθρωποι, ζώα, γεωργικά χωράφια – τα πάντα έχουν πληγεί σοβαρά», λέει ο Dakshina, κάτοικος της Nazira στο Assam που είδε τις πλημμύρες. «Δεν υπήρχαν δρόμοι, ούτε γέφυρες, ούτε προσβάσιμες διαδρομές γιατί τα πάντα ήταν βυθισμένα στο νερό». Όταν τα νερά της πλημμύρας καταπίνουν δρόμους, καλύπτουν γέφυρες και περιβάλλουν ολόκληρους οικισμούς, ζητώντας βοήθεια στο p…
items.descriptionOriginal: "People, animals, agricultural fields – everything has been severely affected," says Dakshina, a resident of Nazira in Assam who witnessed the floods. "There were no roads, no bridges, and no accessible routes because everything was submerged in water." When floodwaters swallow roads, cover bridges and surround entire settlements, getting help to people becomes a race against time. In Assam, where communities face recurring floods, even getting essential supplies to stranded residents can become a challenge. During the recent floods in Upper Assam, parts of Sivasagar and other affected districts faced precisely this problem. Water had cut off communities from the road network, and in some places, even boats struggled to reach people because the water was too shallow. For residents, the uncertainty was frightening. People had to find safer ground while trying to save their livestock and livelihoods. Some were stranded in places where rescue teams could not easily reach them. In this situation, Drones Tech Lab, a deep-tech company incubated at the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Guwahati, deployed payload-carrying drones to deliver food, water, medicines and other essentials across three districts in Assam. The operation reached more than 1,000 people in locations where even conventional relief efforts faced access constraints. The drones also helped survey affected areas and identify stranded residents, giving relief and rescue teams a clearer picture of where assistance was needed. For Dakshina, the intervention revealed a side of drone technology she had never seen before. When floodwaters cut off roads and bridges, drones helped deliver essential supplies to communities stranded in Assam. "Usually, we know drones as something used for taking videos at parties, weddings, or similar events," she says. "But this time, we saw for the first time how drones can actually help people during a disaster." Behind this intervention was technology that had taken years to develop , test and adapt for India's challenging terrain. 'We wanted India to build its own drones' Founded in 2016 by Ritesh Kanu, Biswajit Dey and Debajit Deka, Drones Tech Lab began with a vision to develop indigenous drone capabilities in a country that relied heavily on foreign technology. At the time, India's drone ecosystem was still taking shape. Awareness of its applications beyond photography was limited, access to funding was difficult, and building hardware-intensive technology came with significant challenges. Kanu says the founders wanted to address the dependence on imported systems and build technology suited to India's operational needs. "India has been a consumer of drone technology right from the start," he says. "We had a belief and a vision that we should be building in assets." For the team, indigenous technology did not mean manufacturing every component locally from day one. It meant developing intellectual property, designing system architecture, integrating software and engineering drones for specific missions. Their early work was influenced by the challenges faced by defence personnel operating in difficult environments. The founders saw how technology could help reduce risks to human life, particularly when information about a location or threat was difficult to obtain. Through its association with IIT Guwahati, the company developed unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), flight systems, software and specialised payload mechanisms. Developed at IIT Guwahati, Drones Tech Lab's heavy-payload drone can carry up to 30 kg, with applications ranging from disaster response to healthcare logistics. One of its developments was a heavy-payload drone with an indigenous carbon-fibre frame capable of carrying up to 30 kg. The company has since worked across disaster response, defence, healthcare logistics, mapping, conservation and infrastructure. Kanu compares a drone's carbon-fibre frame to a car's chassis: it holds the different components together. Its propulsion system, which includes motors and electronic speed controllers, provides the force needed to lift and move the drone. The real capability, however, lies in how these components work together. By modifying software, propulsion systems and payload-release mechanisms, the team can adapt a drone to the requirements of a particular mission. During a flood , that could mean carrying essential supplies to a settlement cut off by water. A drone can take help to floot-hit villages The first challenge during a flood is understanding what is happening on the ground. Which settlements are cut off? Where are people stranded? Which areas need supplies most urgently? And how can rescue teams approach them safely? Drones can survey affected areas from above, helping teams map isolated pockets and prioritise their response. Once a delivery point is identified, its coordinates can be entered into the flight plan. The drone then carries the supplies to the designated location, where the package is released for people on the ground to collect. During the Assam operation , Drones Tech Lab used drones with a payload capacity of around 5 kg per flight. They travelled approximately 5 km on missions that took about 25 minutes. The smaller payload was a deliberate choice based on the conditions. "We have drones that can carry more than 50 kilos also," says Kanu. "But the situation demanded a drone with a payload capacity of around 5 kg to make the operation more effective." The process involved much more than flying an aircraft. The team mapped affected locations, coordinated with government officials, prepared supply packets and identified suitable delivery points. Local authorities helped the team reach launch locations and coordinate its work with relief efforts. During the Assam floods, the team used drones carrying around 5 kg per flight, covering approximately 5 km in 25 minutes. Together, these steps helped the team plan where supplies needed to go and how to get them there. Drones also helped responders understand the condition of stranded residents. Dakshina recalls how aerial surveys identified people on rooftops or trapped alongside their livestock, while providing information about water levels and possible routes for rescue teams. When immediate physical rescue was not possible, aerial assessments helped teams determine whether people had food and water and needed urgent assistance. Every disaster taught them something new The company had already deployed its technology during the 2022 Assam floods and following Cyclone Amphan in West Bengal's Sundarbans. Each operation offered lessons in mapping affected areas, locating stranded communities and improving the software used to plan missions. "It's not just a camera drone being flown and then dropping food material somewhere," says Kanu. "The most important thing is that it has to be effective, and that comes only when you have the data." The drones also conducted aerial surveys, helping rescue teams identify people stranded on rooftops and locate areas requiring urgent assistance. He explains that repeated field deployments have helped the team improve how it analyses affected areas and identifies locations that should be prioritised. The goal is to reduce the time between identifying a need and delivering assistance. The company's work extends beyond floods , too. Drones Tech Lab has worked with the Kolkata Municipal Corporation on dengue-control and medicine-spraying operations, supported aerial monitoring and surveillance at Kaziranga National Park, and undertaken healthcare logistics work with AIIMS using payload drones. Each of these applications requires the team to adapt its software, equipment and flight operations to the work being done on the ground. How can drones reach people faster next time? The work also draws on the ecosystem around IIT Guwahati, where Professor Parameshwar K. Iyer is associated with the Centre for Drone Technology. Iyer says efforts to strengthen the region's drone ecosystem gained momentum during the pandemic, when disaster management discussions highlighted the need for interdisciplinary solutions. Facilities for testing drones and training pilots became an important part of that effort. IIT Guwahati established designated areas for drone testing and operations, helping create infrastructure for companies and researchers working in the Northeast. The importance of having this infrastructure in place became clear during the recent Assam floods, when the response had to move quickly. After discussions with the team and state authorities, the drones and personnel were sent to Sivasagar overnight. Within 24 hours, the team was on the ground, surveying affected areas and helping identify stranded residents. For Iyer, the larger question is how such capabilities can be made available before the next emergency. "We have to be ready for any kind of disaster," he says. For communities cut off by floodwaters, drones offered a way to receive essential supplies and help rescue teams locate people waiting for assistance. Photograph: ( Hindustan Times ) He believes establishing drone facilities and services at multiple locations across vulnerable regions could reduce response times and help assistance reach communities faster. Such preparedness would require coordination between technology providers, local administrations and disaster-management agencies. Drones cannot replace evacuation teams, medical care or the wider relief network communities depend on. They can, however, help responders understand what is happening in areas that are difficult to reach and deliver limited supplies while further assistance is organised. 'They had lost hope of receiving relief' For Kanu, the impact of the Assam deployment was best understood through the reactions of people receiving help, rather than the distances flown or the weight carried by the drones. He remembers how some residents had lost hope of receiving relief because no one could easily reach them. Seeing supplies arrive by drone was an unfamiliar experience. "They had actually lost hope of receiving relief because they had no access to it," he says. "When we look back at the work we have put into building this company over the past 10 years, moments like these show us why we started. We may be sitting in Calcutta, working on technology day and night, but seeing it reach people who need help makes that journey worthwhile." As disasters continue to test communities and emergency services, drones offer one way to bridge the gap between those who need help and those trying to reach them. How effectively they can do this depends on their ability to work alongside relief teams on the ground. In Assam, technology developed over nearly a decade found an urgent purpose: carrying essential supplies across flooded terrain to people waiting for help. The next step is ensuring that when roads disappear again, the teams, infrastructure and coordination needed to respond are already in place. The team's efforts brought essential supplies and hope to communities cut off by the floods. For Dakshina, the experience is reason enough to make the technology available in more places. She hopes drones can help locate people and animals in danger and direct assistance towards areas that remain difficult to access. "I sincerely hope that such systems and technologies will be made available in more places," she says. All images courtesy Drones Tech Lab team

items.descriptionOriginal: Visitors to London’s British Museum can admire a remarkable example of Roman ingenuity that’s considered one of the seven glass wonders of the world. Dated to the fourth century, the ornate Lycurgus Cup is a soft jade green — or a striking ruby red, depending on where the light source is positioned. The goblet’s color-changing capability has long perplexed scientists. No one is sure exactly how it was created, but the consensus is that Romans added tiny bits of gold and silver to their glass mixture, forming layers of nanoparticles that interact with light differently depending on their size and shape. Experts had struggled to devise a reliable method of re-creating the material in quantity, but now, for the first time, the mystery appears to have been solved. Melding an ancient recipe with modern science, a glass specialist from the University of Sheffield has reproduced the effect, and commissioned a sculpture that pays homage to the original. Lisa Hollands, with the institution’s School of Chemical, Materials, and Biological Engineering, took on the challenge, which was “very much a labor of love,” per a news release from the university. She worked with a Roman glass expert to develop a base that mimicked those used nearly two millennia ago, then set about experimenting with different furnace types, oxygen levels, and more. She said she knew it would be a much more complicated task than simply sprinkling some gold and silver nanoparticles into a mixture, but did think at one point, “If the Romans could have seen me experimenting, they’d probably laugh and ask: ‘Why does she not know how to make this?’” Finally, Hollands landed on a recipe for glass that looked opaque green under reflected light but red when a light was shone directly on it. “To me, it’s magic,” she told The Guardian . So how exactly does it work? “White light is made up of many different colors and you see this when there is a rainbow in the sky. Nanoparticles are much smaller than the wavelengths of light and in certain conditions they block certain colors due to the light affecting the electrons in the atoms,” she explained to the outlet. “So, for this glass, if light is shone through it, the gold and silver particles block blue and green light, only allowing reds and oranges to pass through. If light is reflected off the surface, the particles have the effect of scattering the light, giving the opaque green color we see,” she continued. Hollands and her project manager approached U.K. glass artist Elliot Walker, who won Season 2 of Netflix’s Blown Away , to create a finished piece that could be exhibited at Sheffield’s upcoming Festival of the Mind, which runs Nov. 6-15. It will then go on permanent display at the university’s Turner Museum of Glass . “You can really get an idea of how the glass makers of the past would have adapted to this sort of glass; it’s like shaking their hands,” Walker said in the release. The Lycurgus Cup depicts the legend of King Lycurgus from Homer’s Iliad , showing the triumph of the Greek god Dionysus over the lawgiver Lycurgus . The 2026 homage bridges the time between the Roman artwork and now. “I wanted to keep the sculpture quite classical in form and to carry through the original story of Lycurgus shown on the cup, but we needed a blown element within this to really show the dichroic glass ,” said Walker. “The piece is a blend of the Lycurgus story and the Farnese Atlas sculpture , with the globe replaced by a cup.” RELATED: Researchers Re-Create 5,000-Year-Old Egyptian Blue, the World’s Oldest Synthetic Pigment Once Lost to Science

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News How to Get Your Riverside, Alabama Home Ready for Summer Heat Reading Time: 6 minutes How to Get Your Riverside, Alabama Home Ready for Summer Heat Key Takeaways Simple preseason checks can uncover cooling problems before hotter weather arrives in Riverside. Clean filters, clear vents, and an unobstructed outdoor unit support steady airflow and comfort. Homeowners can handle basic upkeep, but electrical, refrigerant, and internal equipment repairs are best left to trained technicians. A heatwave backup plan helps protect people, pets, and essential supplies if cooling or power is lost. Summer heat can quickly make a Riverside, Alabama, home feel uncomfortable when an air conditioner is not ready for longer daily run times. Preparing early gives you time to identify basic airflow issues, clear outdoor equipment, and arrange an expert AC tune up Riverside homeowners may need before demand for service increases. The goal is not to disassemble your HVAC system. Instead, focus on safe, visible maintenance tasks that help your home retain cooled air and reveal signs that deserve professional attention. Taking notes as you inspect the system can also be useful. Record unusual sounds, odors, water, uneven room temperatures, or thermostat behavior so you can describe the issue clearly if service is needed later. Why Summer Preparation Matters When temperatures rise, an air conditioner must remove heat from indoors for longer periods. A clogged filter, a blocked return grille, a drainage issue, or a struggling component may be less noticeable in mild weather but become much more apparent during the first sustained hot spell. Preparing before peak heat also reduces the chance that a small concern becomes an urgent comfort problem. Riverside households can also review the practical safety guidance in the EPA’s information on extreme heat as they make their summer plans. Preparation also makes it easier to distinguish between a minor comfort issue and a problem that requires prompt attention. For example, a room that has always received intense afternoon sun may need better shading. In contrast, a room that suddenly has low airflow could indicate an obstructed vent, a filter issue, or equipment failure. Addressing visible issues early can help avoid unnecessary stress during high outdoor temperatures. The Homeowner Cooling Checklist Set aside a short amount of time to walk through this list before summer settles in: Inspect or replace the air filter. Move furniture, rugs, and curtains away from supply vents and return grilles. Remove leaves, grass clippings, and loose debris around the outdoor unit. Test the thermostat in cooling mode. Look for water near the indoor equipment. Listen for unusual sounds when the system starts. Schedule service if you find warning signs. As you complete the checklist, avoid making multiple adjustments at once. Change or inspect the filter, confirm that vents are open, and then allow the system time to operate normally. This approach makes it easier to notice whether a particular step improved comfort or whether the concern remains. Keep access paths to both indoor and outdoor equipment clear so a technician can inspect the system safely if an appointment becomes necessary. Check Filters and Airflow A dirty filter restricts airflow, which can reduce cooling effectiveness and place additional strain on the system. Use the filter size and type specified for your equipment, and inspect it regularly. Homes with pets, ongoing renovations, heavy dust, or household members with allergy concerns may need more frequent checks. Keep supply vents open, and ensure that sofas, bookcases, curtains, or storage bins do not cover the return grilles. A filter should capture airborne particles without being so restrictive that it reduces the airflow your system needs. When checking a filter, make sure it is installed in the correct direction. Many filters include an arrow that should point toward the equipment and in the direction of airflow. Also, look at the filter rack or access door after replacing it; a poorly seated filter can leave gaps that allow unfiltered air and dust to bypass the filter. Clear the Outdoor Unit The outdoor portion of a central air-conditioning system releases heat collected from inside the house. Keep the area around it free of weeds, leaves, grass clippings, and stacked items so air can move around the cabinet. Trim back vegetation that crowds the unit, while avoiding aggressive cutting or contact with the equipment. After mowing or yard work, take a quick look at the area around the unit. Grass clippings and loose debris can collect against the cabinet or around the base. Avoid placing lawn tools, trash containers, decorations, or storage items next to the equipment, even temporarily, because they can limit airflow and make future inspection more difficult. Do not open electrical panels, straighten thin metal fins, or spray the unit with high-pressure water. Damaged wiring, severe corrosion, bent fins, or obvious physical damage are reasons to stop and arrange a professional inspection. Test the Thermostat Set the thermostat to cooling mode. Choose a setting below the current indoor temperature. Allow several minutes for a normal startup delay. Confirm that cool air reaches the main living spaces. Replace batteries if the display is fading, blank, or unresponsive. Setting the thermostat far below your desired temperature does not make the system cool faster. It simply calls for a longer cooling cycle, which can increase energy use. If your thermostat has a schedule or programmable settings, review them before the hottest part of the season. Confirm that the programmed temperatures match the household’s routine and that vacation or away settings have not been left on accidentally. Keep the thermostat area clear of lamps, electronics, and direct sunlight when possible, as nearby heat can affect the device’s readings. Reduce Heat Inside the Home Good cooling performance depends on more than the equipment; close blinds, drapes, or shades on windows that receive strong morning or afternoon sun. Keep exterior doors closed during the hottest part of the day, and use ovens, dryers, and other heat-producing appliances during cooler hours when practical. Check for obvious gaps around doors and windows, then repair damaged weatherstripping or seals. Ceiling fans can make people feel cooler by moving air across the skin, but they do not lower the room’s actual temperature. Over the longer term, attic insulation, air sealing, and duct repairs can help limit unwanted heat gain. For best comfort, use ceiling fans only in occupied rooms and turn them off when the room is empty. If a particular room consistently feels warmer, compare it with the rest of the home at different times of day. Closing window coverings before direct sunlight enters the room, keeping doors positioned to support airflow, and avoiding heat-producing activities there can make a noticeable difference without changing the thermostat for the entire house. Know When to Call a Professional Leave refrigerant work, capacitor testing, electrical repairs, internal coil access, and major drainage repairs to a qualified HVAC professional. These tasks can involve electrical hazards, specialized tools, and components that should not be handled casually. A professional should also evaluate recurring problems rather than just the most visible symptom. For instance, repeatedly changing a filter will not correct a persistent drainage problem, an electrical fault, a damaged component, or a duct issue. If the system has a history of short-cycling, uneven cooling, or water near the equipment, note when the problem occurs and whether it has become more frequent. Warning Signs That Need Attention Warm air or weak airflow from multiple vents. Repeated breaker trips. Water is pooling near indoor equipment. Grinding, buzzing, rattling, burning, or strong musty odors. Frequent starts and stops. A noticeable, unexplained increase in energy use. What a Professional Inspection May Cover A service visit may include electrical safety checks, airflow and temperature testing, thermostat operation, condensate-drain evaluation, inspection of coils and components, and refrigerant-system testing when needed. Before the appointment, make a list of the symptoms you have noticed, including which rooms feel different and whether the issue occurs at a certain time of day. If possible, note whether the problem started suddenly or developed gradually. These details can help the technician understand the situation and focus the inspection on likely causes. Create a Heatwave Plan Choose a room that can serve as a temporary comfort space if the main system has trouble. Keep drinking water, medications, phone chargers, flashlights, and battery-powered fans accessible. Know which nearby public locations may offer air conditioning, and check on older adults, young children, people with health conditions, and pets. It is also helpful to decide in advance who will be responsible for checking on family members, neighbors, or friends who may be more vulnerable to heat. Keep important contact numbers available in case cellular devices need to be conserved. If you use medical equipment that depends on electricity, discuss backup arrangements and emergency planning needs with the appropriate health care provider or equipment supplier before severe heat arrives. During dangerous heat, portable fans may improve comfort but cannot prevent heat illness in very hot rooms. The EPA’s indoor heat safety advice also recommends using generators outdoors and at least 20 feet away from buildings, doors, windows, and vents. Common Questions When should I prepare my cooling system? Start before the first extended stretch of hot weather. Early preparation leaves more time to address a problem without waiting through a peak-season service rush. It also allows you to test the thermostat and cooling operation when the home does not yet rely on the system for all-day use. How often should I change an air filter? Follow the equipment maker’s guidance and inspect the filter regularly. Replacement timing depends on the filter type, household conditions, pets, dust, and system use. A visual inspection is often more useful than relying only on a calendar reminder, especially during periods of heavier system use. Why is one room hotter than the rest of the house? Common causes include direct sun exposure, blocked vents, dirty filters, duct leakage, inadequate insulation, and airflow or equipment problems. Start with simple checks, such as window coverings and blocked vents, then seek professional advice if the difference persists or affects several rooms. What if the AC stops during a heatwave? Check thermostat settings, batteries, the filter, and whether a breaker has tripped once. Do not keep resetting a breaker that trips again. If indoor temperatures climb, move people and pets to a cooler location and call a qualified professional. Final Steps Before Summer A few early checks can make a Riverside home more comfortable when summer heat arrives. Handle simple upkeep, keep air moving freely, reduce indoor heat gain, and seek professional help when symptoms suggest electrical, refrigerant, drainage, or mechanical trouble. Preparing your home and household plan before the hottest days arrive can make it easier to respond calmly if comfort problems occur. items.descriptionOriginal: Episode Description: Two coral fragments fell over in a Stanford lab tank and happened to touch, and within days the bleached one started absorbing healthy algae directly through the contact point with its neighbor. The researchers hadn’t designed that experiment, which is part of what makes the discovery so striking: a potential recovery mechanism for bleached coral hiding in plain sight, requiring nothing more than the right genetic match and direct physical contact. Arielle and Karissa cover ten solutions this week, including a brain therapy reporting 68 percent remission for PTSD when decades of medication have only reached 11, a wildlife sanctuary in Austin that runs on Twitch donations and reaches the conservation audience that broadcast nature documentaries never could, and the solar panels now legal for California renters that require no contractor, no roof, and no tens of thousands of dollars upfront. If you have questions, comments, feedback, suggestions, or just want to say hi, send a message to: podcast@optimistdaily.com . Want to be part of the Optimism Movement? Become an Emissary . Subscribe to our FREE Daily/Weekly Newsletter and follow us on Instagram , X , and Blue Sky . The Optimist Daily is a project of the World Business Academy. Karissa: And I’m Karissa. Arielle: And welcome back to The Optimist Daily’s weekly roundup. How are you, Karissa? Karissa: Um, feeling pretty tired. Trying to adjust to the time change here, so. Arielle: Oh, yeah. You guys had your time change in the States this past weekend, right? Karissa: Mm-hmm. Yeah, and I know you had it the weekend before. But yeah, this week has been, been all about adjustment. Arielle: It’s a bit of a transition period. I feel like a lot of my friends are going through transitions right now, and it kind of aligns with the seasons. And also Thanksgiving is coming up. Well, I mean, Canadian Thanksgiving already happened in October, and that’s what I grew up with. But you guys have your Thanksgiving soon. And, uh, to celebrate, we’re doing our local changemaker series like we do every year. Karissa: Yeah, it’s always one of our favorite times of year, too, to give back to The Optimist Daily community and report on the changemakers that are making a difference in your lives and your communities. Speaking of gratitude, we’re very grateful for all of you Optimists who keep The Optimist Daily going in our shared resolve to get positive news out there. And we also wanna thank our Emissaries, who are the financial supporters of The Optimist Daily. Arielle: We have big love for our Emissaries. They help us keep the lights on here. But there are a lot of free ways that you can help support this mission as well, ’cause we know that not everybody has the budget to donate, and that’s completely fine. But if you wanted to help our cause in other ways, you can follow us on socials. We are @optimistdaily on everything except for X. There we are @OdeToOptimism. And along with that, you can share our content on your own personal stories or send them directly to friends and family who you think need a little bit more positivity in their lives. All of that helps us out a lot. Karissa: You can also email us at podcast@optimistdaily.com, or reach out to us on any of the platforms we’re on. Arielle: All right. Well, with all of that said and done, I think I’m going to jump into this week’s solutions. Sardinian restaurants banning phones Arielle: The first one is titled “Sardinian restaurants are banning phones for families at meals”. So in Sardinia, 15 restaurants are asking families to put their phones away when they sit down to eat. In exchange, staff hand them a box of games designed by pediatricians to help parents and kids actually talk to each other. Do you find yourself either seeing people out at a restaurant who aren’t actually engaging with each other ’cause they’re on their phones, or do you find yourself doing that as well, Karissa? Karissa: I mean, I definitely see people doing it, and I try my hardest not to do it. Usually when I’m out at dinner it’s with someone maybe I haven’t seen in a while, so we have lots to talk about, so really try not to. But I, I mean, I can be guilty sometimes if I’m just out at dinner, um, with maybe my family or my boyfriend because, you know, we’re talking all the time, so I’m like, “Well, let me just pull it out for a second while we’re waiting.” Arielle: Yeah, I try my best to just keep my phone, um, where I can’t see it when I’m with other people. Yeah. But I… If I’m eating by myself then I will- Karissa: Mm. Arielle: … um, distract myself with my phone, you know? What I like about this screen time story is that it’s a little bit different from the typical one that you see. It’s not, like, just a lecture or, or, like, a rule. There’s actually a- Yeah … kit. It’s a pediatrician-designed game box that the restaurant itself will hand you so that you have something in your hands other than a phone. So that to me is, like, a structural solution and not so much of a moral one. Or it is, but, like, there’s more structure to it. Karissa: Yeah. Arielle: Anna Cau, she’s the Children’s Ombudsman, which is an independent official appointed to receive, investigate, and help resolve complaints made by individuals against government agencies, public authorities, or private organizations, if you didn’t know. That I got from Wikipedia. But she’s the woman who designed the scheme, and she makes this point: Most screen time debates put the whole problem on parents, and she’s saying the spaces families move through, like restaurants and anywhere in public life, they should also be part of the solution. Karissa: Yeah. Arielle: And this is based in Sardinia, uh, which is in Italy. And there, the communal meal carries a lot of cultural weight. Yeah. I mean, it carries weight everywhere because eating is such a social human practice. But in Italy especially, if the- Karissa: Yeah … Arielle: dinner table is losing to screens over there, then that’s a, a real signal. So yeah, I just really enjoyed reading about this solution, and maybe it will inspire other people who are listening to have their own kind of phone-free dinners. And, uh, you know, I’m sure you can look up engaging questions online or create your own questions to ask your family members as well. You don’t need to have this, uh, specific game box or pediatrician-designed kit. California balcony solar for renters Arielle: The next solution is titled “California legalizes balcony solar for renters and beyond”. We’ve been hearing a lot about solar energy and apartment dwellers being able to participate in that, but this is quite local to you, Karissa, ’cause California just legalized plug-in solar panels, and for the first time, that includes renters. Panels that cost a few hundred dollars that you hang off your balcony or stick outside a window that could cut your electricity bill by up to $500 a year are now legal. So there’s no contractor, no roof, no tens of thousands of dollars upfront for Californians who live in apartments. California is the 10th state to pass this kind of law. It’s the biggest electricity market in the country, so when California moves, then manufacturers basically have to follow. The goal advocates keep describing is plug-in solar on a shelf at a hardware store like any other appliance, and that’s finally a realistic near-term thing. First green star discovered Arielle: The next solution is a pretty fun one. It’s titled “Astronomers discovered first green star ever, and it’s powered by a dead planet’s chemistry”. Astronomers just found the first green star ever documented, a white dwarf that glows chartreuse, not because of temperature, but because it absorbed sodium from a planetary system it destroyed. A star that ate its planets and turned green. It’s like a sci-fi. I was just- Yeah … fascinated by this whole solution. We’ve always assumed star colors track with temperature, like iron heating in a blacksmith’s forge, if you can imagine, like, it goes from red to white hot, and this star kind of broke that model. Its color is a chemical record of what it’s consumed. Carbon-rich atmospheres glow pink or purple. Stars that absorbed asteroid or planetary material go yellow. But then this one went green. There’s a lot more on the science within the article itself. Uh, but yeah, I just found the whole thing quite interesting. I just think it’s really cool to think about all of this unexpected, completely surprising stuff happening in this universe. Great Koala National Park Arielle: Okay, moving on to the next solution, which is titled, “How carbon credits helped unlock the Great Koala National Park in New South Wales, Australia.” After more than a decade of campaigning, three state elections, and 14 hours of parliamentary debate, Australia’s Great Koala National Park is officially real. It’s 478,000 hectares of protected habitat, which is roughly 1.2 million acres, and the thing that finally made it financially viable was carbon credits. The part about carbon credits is what makes the economics work. The government registered over 117,000 hectares of the park state forests with the Federal Clean Energy Regulator. By ending native forest logging there, they can now sell carbon credits from the land. Protected forest generates more revenue than logged timber, it turns out, and that’s the financial argument that helped get this through. The article goes into the human cost. It didn’t wanna glaze over that detail. The forestry corporation already cut 30-plus jobs in Coffs Harbour before the park was even finalized, and then there’s also timber suppliers and trucking companies, engineering firms, all of these places of employment that have to let a lot of people go. So the government- Yeah … is committed to moving displaced workers into national parks roles, but that transition is still underway, and I’m sure it will go through some growing pains. Ashley Love, the conservationist who started this campaign after locals told him koalas weren’t as common as they used to be, called the result, “Quite fragmented with connectivity gaps still to close.” But he’s already pushing for the sections that didn’t make it into the park. And yeah, after a decade, he sounds less frustrated than just persistent, because this is still such an accomplishment. Karissa: Conservation campaigns that connect land protection to economic logic are always gonna be more viable. I think it’s a good model to follow, and, um, just a, a win for the koalas. Arielle: Mm-hmm. It’s a win for the koalas, and a win for Australia’s broader biodiversity as a whole. Coral healing through touch Arielle: The last solution that I’m going to share with everyone before I hand over the reins to Karissa is “Stanford scientists discovered bleached coral can heal through touch”. Two coral fragments accidentally fell over and touched each other in a Stanford lab tank. Within days, the fragment that was bleached started recovering, absorbing healthy algae directly through the point of contact with the healthy coral fragment. The researchers were blown away because this was not supposed to happen. It was not really their experiment at all. What makes it scientifically interesting is how specific the conditions have to be for this to happen. It only works with direct physical contact and only between genetically identical corals. If you separate them by a few millimeters, then nothing will happen. If you introduce a different genetic background, then they reject each other, much like a mismatched organ transplant. Genetic twins in contact create what the team calls a tissue bridge, which is a nutrient highway between them The IUCN announced that about 96% of the world’s shallow water reef systems are critically endangered and could disappear by 2075. Coral reefs support between a quarter and a third of all marine species, so this discovery is a glimmer of hope in a very dark picture. Maya Higa’s wildlife sanctuary on Twitch Karissa: Okay, so this is one of our local Change Makers series articles, and it’s about Maya Higa, who built a wildlife sanctuary on Twitch funded by the people who watch it. Earlier this year, Maya was on a trip to Dominica and was offered the chance to swim with sperm whales, and she said no. Her followers couldn’t be there, and that one decision pretty much captures what she built Alveus Sanctuary to do and explains how a Twitch stream became a $7.5 million conservation platform. Alveus is both a physical wildlife sanctuary in Austin and a virtual conservation classroom. Animal ambassadors, animals that can’t survive in the wild, live at the sanctuary, while a 24/7 live stream lets viewers watch, learn, and get to know individual animals by name. And Maya’s background isn’t just as a creator. She’s a former zookeeper with a falconry license and a licensed wildlife rehabilitator. So all that knowledge is what this stream runs on. The demographic she’s reaching is one that traditional conservation has struggled to reach for decades. She’s reaching 18 to 30-year-olds through social media in ways that broadcast nature documentaries never could. Arielle: Yeah, it’s such a smart move. You know, a lot of the time the depiction of the younger generation is that their attention spans are really, um, short, which in some ways is true, but there’s also a lot of young people who just love to watch streams, and those are like- Yeah … long-form, like the longest form content there is. So yeah, really big shout-out to Maya. This is an incredible project. And yeah, I, I think I’m gonna start watching … the animals as well. Karissa: I love this whole idea, and of course they’re targeting the younger viewers, but I think it kind of reaches across the ages as well. Um, my mind goes to in California, Jackie and Shadow, the bald eagles that- Yeah lived in Big Bear Lake, I think captured the hearts of many. So once again, congrats to Maya, and check out the article for more details. Solar kits for disaster relief Karissa: The next solution is “Solar kits are changing what disaster relief looks like”. Every morning in a refugee camp in Bangladesh, Mohammed Saber climbs to the roof of his family’s bamboo and tarpaulin shelter and puts out a solar panel. He’s done it for six years since his family fled the Rohingya crackdown in Myanmar. That one panel is how his whole family charges phones, cooks with light, and keeps fans running through the heat. And this story is about what this technology is actually for. The range of where this is happening right now is pretty striking. Doctors Without Borders is running a tuberculosis clinic on solar in Karachi, and UN water filtration on solar in South Sudan. And kits were distributed after Nepal’s floods that killed over 1,400 people. And a nonprofit in Ukraine has given kits to thousands of families, including 75 and 80-year-old grandparents who just plug them in. The CEO said, “It’s just a matter of plug and play for these solar relief kits.” And I mean, that goes back to our earlier solution of the plug-in balcony solar panels. But switching from diesel to solar is harder than it sounds for aid organizations because long-running generator contracts are still going on. There’s new distribution chains that have to be navigated in genuinely dangerous conditions. In addition, recent donor funding cuts have made it harder to transition to new technology. So one program leader said flat out, “Much of the technical expertise in the humanitarian sector on energy has been cut.” Arielle: Yeah, it’s interesting. Whenever I think about solar panels, I think about the types of solutions that we’ve been hearing about so far, like the rooftop solar in Australia for apartments or the plug-in solar or solar panels above farm fields. But I don’t really think about it in this context where it could be so, so useful for disaster relief or- Yeah for places that don’t have access to a reliable grid. Uh, so I think it’s really encouraging that this technology is reaching all corners of the world for all types of contexts and situations. Household uses for toothpaste Karissa: The next story is a lifestyle solution, and it’s “Eight surprising household uses for toothpaste from a pro cleaner”. So there’s probably a tube of toothpaste in your bathroom right now, and if it’s only going on your teeth, you’re leaving a surprisingly useful cleaning tool just sitting in the drawer. A professional cleaner shared the eight household jobs she regularly uses it for, and some of them are actually not that obvious. Plain, white, non-gel toothpaste has mild abrasive particles that work like an ultra-fine sandpaper, and that’s why it can buff out light scratches on glass, phone screens, and wood surfaces, and polish metal fixtures, so lots of different uses. Gel toothpaste doesn’t have those particles, so it doesn’t work the same way, and that’s just something to keep in mind when you reach for that toothpaste. One use I was surprised to read is using toothpaste for a fogged car headlight, and it’s one that a lot of people haven’t heard, and it’s really simple. You just rub toothpaste over the lens in small circles for about a minute or two, rinse, dry, and repeat if needed. So no specialty product is required to clear up those fogged headlights. There’s just kind of this huge appetite right now, especially with the economy and the whole idea of sustainability as well, to, you know, use things you already own and get creative with them. It’s practical, it’s low cost, and it’s also satisfying as well. Brain therapy for PTSD Karissa: Moving on to the next solution, “Personalized brain therapy hits 68% remission for PTSD”. The best FDA-approved medications for PTSD have a remission rate of about 11%. But a newly FDA-cleared brain therapy just reported a 68% remission, and that’s not a typo. That is a big difference. It’s the first non-drug treatment specifically cleared for PTSD since the diagnosis was formally recognized in 1980. How this therapy works is that you get an EEG that maps your specific brain electrical activity, and an AI algorithm builds a personalized stimulation plan from that data. Then a coil placed against your scalp delivers targeted magnetic pulses, and you do this for five sessions a week for five to six weeks. The lead researcher described standard brain stimulation as covering the leak with a tarp, and this treatment tries to find and replace the damaged shingles. This is important for many different populations because about 6% of Americans will experience PTSD in their lifetime with higher rates among women and veterans. Approximately 17.5 veterans die by suicide each day in the US. The two SSRIs approved for PTSD have been the only FDA-approved options since 1980, and 11% remission means the vast majority haven’t gotten there on medications alone. So this is a really great breakthrough, and of course, accessibility is going to be the next hurdle. Um, you know, teams are actively trying to work on getting this covered by insurance, and FDA clearance is not the same as accessibility, so this gap is the next fight Volunteering this Thanksgiving Karissa: The final solution I have to share is “The best places to volunteer this Thanksgiving, 17 options for every schedule”. Every year around Thanksgiving, a lot of people have the same thought, “This is the year I actually do something.” And then they show up at a food bank and find out every other person in town had the same idea. There’s actually a smarter way to do this, and several options that don’t even require leaving your couch at all. So I think the most important point out of this article, even though it gives tips to volunteer and help around, is that holiday demand often creates more volunteers than organizations can actually use on Thanksgiving Day itself. And a lot of that is directed at food banks. So if you want your time to count, definitely call ahead and see if you’re needed. And if you get redirected because a location is at capacity, ask when they need people the most. The answer is almost always in February, when the holiday energy has faded out, but the need hasn’t. And I think that’s just a really good point. These organizations need your help year-round, and that’s important to keep in mind. So this list covers every kind of situation, whether it’s Feeding America, Meals on Wheels, and Operation Turkey, and about the tightly organized shifts they have. But it also covers options that are remote, like writing letters to deployed service members through Support Our Troops, and animal shelters for people who are better with dogs than crowds. So lots of ways to volunteer this giving, thankful, grateful season. So yeah, I think it’s just a great reminder, and hard to believe that Thanksgiving is already around the corner. Arielle: Yeah, I totally agree. I, I didn’t really think too much about the oversaturation in the volunteering space for the holiday season. It does make sense, though. So, you know, I, I think if you’re interested in volunteering and just haven’t gotten around to it yet, then maybe the holiday season is a great place to start. But then it could be your gateway into doing it- Karissa: Yeah … Arielle: more regularly as well. Outro & quote Karissa: Well, that’s all of the positive news we had to share this week on The Optimist Daily. But before we go, we’ll leave you off with a quote. ” Arielle: Having a good time together is the essence of lovingness and the best means of increasing it.” That’s from Benjamin Spock, and I think that’s a great quote to go with quite a few of our stories today. Karissa: Yeah, exactly. That’s why I wanted to include it in today’s, uh, roundup. Arielle: We will be back next week with more solutions. In the meantime, Karissa and I wish all of you Optimists and Emissaries a wonderful weekend. Karissa: Yeah. Bye, everyone. Arielle: Bye. The post Podcast Transcript November 6th, 2026— 2 coral fragments touched in a Stanford lab: a story of healing (plus 9 more solutions) first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .

items.descriptionOriginal: A firecracker goes off at the end of a residential lane. A dog sleeping beside a parked car suddenly gets up, its ears alert. Another blast follows. Within seconds, the dog is running, looking for somewhere to hide. It may dart across the road, squeeze beneath a vehicle, or disappear into a nearby construction site. While pet owners can prepare a safe space for their animals at home, street animals have no such protection. They depend on the people living around them to recognise their distress and respond. Speaking to The Better India, Dr Vikas Godara, a small-animal veterinarian and soft-tissue surgeon with over 11 years of clinical experience in India and the United States, including emergency and critical care, explains that the impact of Diwali on animals goes beyond injuries caused directly by firecrackers. He identifies three recurring categories of veterinary cases during the festive season: noise-induced anxiety, firecracker-related injuries, and gastrointestinal complications caused by ingesting discarded food and other objects. Here is why community animals are particularly vulnerable, and what residents can do to make the celebrations safer for them. When the noise becomes a source of fear A dog's hearing is considerably more sensitive than a human's. Sounds that people may dismiss as occasional festive noise can become overwhelming for animals, particularly when firecrackers burst repeatedly and without warning. Unlike humans, dogs cannot understand when a loud sound is likely to occur or when it will stop. The sudden blasts can trigger fear responses, including trembling, hiding, excessive barking, restlessness, and attempts to escape. Repeated exposure to loud noise can cause extreme stress and disorientation. Vulnerable animals may also experience serious physiological distress, including shock and, in severe cases, potentially fatal cardiac complications. Godara, who is also the founder of Vetezy, an online platform providing virtual/video vet consultations and same-day care access for pet parents in India, says, "Veterinary clinics see a noticeable increase in anxiety-related cases around Deepavali. Some dogs stop eating, while others become withdrawn or display signs of extreme fear. Puppies and community dogs can be particularly vulnerable. The impact is not limited to animals that are directly targeted by firecrackers. Even a cracker bursting several metres away can frighten a dog that has nowhere quiet to retr Why street dogs bear the greater burden A pet frightened by fireworks may have a family to comfort it, a familiar room to retreat to and access to veterinary care. A street dog does not necessarily have any of these. Their vulnerability is also reflected in reports from Bengaluru during Deepavali 2025. A report published by The New Indian Express on 24 October 2025 documented 30 – 40 cases received by Mylos Rescue over four to five days, according to its founder, Lakshmi Swaminathan. These included incidents of deliberate cruelty, with dogs' legs reportedly tied with firecrackers. At Charlie's Animal Rescue Centre (CARE) , manager Kirtan Aarti reported that seven to eight dogs had been found dead after being run over by vehicles along Ballari Main Road and the airport flyover while attempting to escape the noise. Animals experiencing severe anxiety need veterinary assessment and, in some cases, anti-anxiety medication. Photograph: (P. Ravikumar, EPS) Little Hearts Animal Healing Rescue Centre, founded by Rajkumar, received approximately 10 cases of cracker-related animal injuries. The incidents were reported from areas including Ullal, Kengeri and Banashankari. These figures offer a glimpse of the risks animals face in urban neighbourhoods. They also point to an important distinction: the consequences of a noisy celebration are not experienced equally. Firecracker injuries are only part of the problem Burns, cuts and other physical injuries are among the immediate dangers of firecrackers. Crackers thrown towards animals can cause burns, while fragments and debris can injure their paws. Repeated exposure to loud blasts can also affect their hearing. Godara says that the veterinary response depends on the nature and severity of each injury. "Every patient needs their own tailored treatment plan," he tells The Better India. Dogs with physical injuries may require wound care, antibiotics and treatment for affected tissue. Animals experiencing severe anxiety need veterinary assessment and, in some cases, anti-anxiety medication. The important thing, he explains, is that treatment cannot follow a single approach for every animal. For residents, this means that an injured or distressed community dog should not simply be left to recover on its own. If an animal has suffered burns, is bleeding, appears disoriented or is struggling to move, people should contact a veterinarian or local animal rescue organisation. Those attempting to help should also avoid handling a frightened or injured animal without taking precautions. An animal in pain may react defensively, even towards someone trying to assist it. The danger that remains after the crackers stop Once the celebrations wind down, another festive-season hazard often goes unnoticed: food waste. "Sweets, leftover food, spoiled offerings and discarded packaging can end up in open spaces, dumping grounds and roadside bins. Community dogs and cattle searching for food may consume these without anyone knowing what they have eaten", he explains. Godara identifies gastrointestinal complications as another recurring concern during the festive period. This problem is not restricted to Diwali. People regularly leave household leftovers for community animals throughout the year. Photograph: (Live Law) "Street dogs and cattle often forage through dumping grounds and open spaces, where they may consume spoiled food or objects that can cause toxicity and gastrointestinal complications." One common misconception, he says, is that feeding sweets to dogs only causes skin problems. "There is a big myth that if you feed sweets to a dog, they would only get a skin issue. But that's not true. They can develop toxicity due to excessive sugar, gastrointestinal upset," he explains. This problem is not restricted to Diwali. People regularly leave household leftovers for community animals throughout the year. However, the quantity of discarded food can increase during festivals, making it more difficult to monitor what animals are consuming. Feeding community dogs needs a little more care Feeding street dogs is often one of the first ways residents express concern for animals in their neighbourhood. But good intentions do not always translate into safe feeding practices. In residential areas, several people may feed the same dogs without coordinating with one another. Food may be left in different locations, sometimes without attention to its ingredients, freshness, or quantity. Godara believes housing societies and neighbourhood groups need to take greater responsibility for monitoring these practices. Referring to designated feeding areas , he says that such spaces need to be monitored to ensure people do not leave sweets, spoiled food or other potentially harmful leftovers. "Even if the laws are in place, how much of them are followed? If somebody is feeding animals at designated areas, you can have someone who actually monitors what is being offered. But the answer is not always yes. Even people who love stray dogs do not necessarily follow these designated feeding practices," he tells The Better India. For him, enforcement alone is not enough. Residents must also understand what constitutes safe feeding. Cruelty is another danger residents must recognise Not every injury suffered by a street animal is accidental. Godara draws attention to cases of deliberate harm and mishandling, including tying rubber bands around animals' limbs, throwing firecrackers at them and physically assaulting them. He describes cases where rubber bands remain embedded in a dog's skin over time, eventually causing wounds as the animal grows. Community dogs may tolerate human handling, but that does not mean they are comfortable or unable to experience pain. "These are injuries induced by human beings. I have seen many horrible examples of mishandling of street dogs. It comes in all forms and shapes," he says. Long guidelines may not always reach the people who interact with street animals every day. Instead, he suggests using short, memorable messages in regional languages that people can understand and repeat. "Once we start talking about awareness, we cannot essentially force it upon anybody. It has to come from within. Something concise, something that sticks in people's heads and gets repeated over and over again, might help," he explains. Such campaigns, he adds, must reach beyond residents who regularly interact with street dogs. Domestic workers, security guards, gardeners, delivery personnel, dog walkers and families living in neighbouring localities are often among those who encounter community animals most frequently. Their participation can make a difference, particularly on nights when firecrackers are being burst across several streets simultaneously. What residents can do for pets and community animals Protecting animals during Diwali does not always require specialist intervention. A few precautions taken before and during the celebrations can reduce their exposure to harm. Alert neighbourhood residents: Inform security guards, domestic workers, delivery personnel and other residents about the risks of bursting crackers near animals. Keep resting spaces safe: Avoid bursting crackers near places where dogs usually sleep or seek shelter. Check beneath parked vehicles before starting them. Provide safe, suitable food and water: Do not feed community dogs sweets, spoiled food or festive leftovers. Ensure that food and water are placed in appropriate, monitored locations. Watch for injured animals: If a dog is bleeding, burnt, limping or showing signs of severe distress, contact a veterinarian or animal rescue group rather than leaving it untreated. Dispose of firecracker waste responsibly: Remove discarded cracker remains and packaging from places where animals forage or walk, while ensuring that debris is handled safely. Coordinate with local feeders and rescuers: Neighbourhood groups can identify vulnerable animals, share emergency contact details and arrange help when required. Collective care can make neighbourhoods safer Godara believes neighbourhood-level participation is essential, including exploring temporary shelters or community-supported spaces where animals can receive care. "Adoption is the only permanent solution, but not everyone will be willing or able to bring a community dog into their home. However, neighbourhoods can still contribute through collective care and support," he says. He emphasises that this cannot be achieved through a single institutional directive. It requires grassroots participation and cooperation. There are already examples of residents and animal welfare groups taking this concern into public spaces. In Kolkata, the West Bengal Animal Rights Activists' Front (WBARAF) , a city-based forum of animal lovers that works to protect, rescue and advocate for community animals, organised a march against the use of illegal and loud firecrackers. More than 100 members, led by the forum's president, actor Sreelekha Mitra, gathered outside the Academy of Fine Arts and marched towards Rashbehari More. Participants carried placards reading 'Let animals live in peace', 'Say no to firecrackers' and 'Celebrate kindness, not noise'. The march highlighted the psychological and physical harm caused to community dogs, cats and birds by loud firecrackers, including hearing damage, disorientation and accidents. For a street dog, a neighbourhood is its home. Its resting place may be a pavement, a space beneath a staircase, or the corner of a residential lane. Photograph: (India Karuna Collaborative) Godara has also noticed a change in the number of injured community animals reaching veterinary clinics over the years. "Initially, I used to see three dogs at my clinic after Diwali. Currently, what I am seeing is 30 dogs. That does not necessarily mean the problem has become worse. The dog population has also increased, and more people are now aware enough to bring them to a veterinarian," he explains. He believes awareness, social media documentation and greater public scrutiny have encouraged people to report cruelty and seek medical attention for injured animals. However, increased reporting does not mean the underlying problems have disappeared. For a street dog, a neighbourhood is its home. Its resting place may be a pavement, a space beneath a staircase, or the corner of a residential lane. It cannot choose to leave when the noise begins. A celebration need not come at the cost of another living being's safety. Sometimes, making room for animals to live through the night in peace begins with not bursting a cracker where they sleep. items.descriptionOriginal: Solar panels above, fish below: That’s the idea behind aquavoltaics, an emerging way to pair solar power with fish farming. Freshwater aquaculture produces more than 160 million tons of fish, crabs, and shrimp a year, emitting an estimated 438 million tons of CO 2 equivalents (tCO 2 eq). A new study finds that covering the world’s aquaculture ponds with floating solar panels could generate nearly as much electricity as the United States uses, far more than enough to offset the industry’s carbon footprint. Photovoltaic electricity is Earth’s most abundant potential source of renewable energy, but it requires lots of surface area. So people have tried to combine it with other types of land use, spawning agrivoltaics , in which solar panels are spaced across farm fields or pastures —harvesting a fraction of the incoming sunlight without appreciably reducing crop yields. People have also tried covering lakes , canals, and reservoirs with photovoltaic panels —but the wildly fluctuating levels and large size of these water bodies present major challenges. Aquaculture ponds , in contrast, are generally small and shallow, with consistent water levels. In the new study, the authors analyzed satellite imagery and other data to estimate the total global area of aquaculture ponds. They identified 50,000 square km of these ponds worldwide, of which only 423 square km currently host water-surface photovoltaics. Some 97 percent of this aquavoltaic area was in China, with most of the rest in Vietnam, South Korea, Thailand, and Israel. .IRPP_ruby , .IRPP_ruby .postImageUrl , .IRPP_ruby .centered-text-area The authors estimated that the electricity generated (4,100 TWhr/yr) could replace enough fossil fuel-derived energy to avoid 2.5 billion tCO 2 eq per year—nearly six times the current emissions of aquaculture worldwide. This electricity production would concentrate along the coastlines of South and East Asia (including Indonesia and the Philippines), with additional hotspots in coastal regions of the Middle East, Egypt, Southern Europe, Central America, Mexico, South America, and the U.S. This locally produced power could cover the current national electricity needs of Vietnam, Indonesia, Bangladesh, Myanmar, the Philippines, Cambodia, Ecuador, Honduras, and Nicaragua. This aquavoltaic energy would be produced in non-industrial regions that are often not well connected to larger power grids—potentially sustaining over 800 small- and medium-sized cities worldwide. These calculations rest on baselines that will need to be refined for different regions, fish and crustacean species—including the assumption that 40 percent coverage of the water surface won’t compromise aquaculture yields. But it raises the possibility that aquavoltaics—a sector that didn’t even exist prior to 2010—could help drive our transition to renewable energy. items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News The Many Ways Student-Led Climate Action Can Look Reading Time: 3 minutes Three Canadian schools doing three completely different projects, all with one common thread. By now, we can see that climate action doesn’t take just one shape. There are so many climate solutions that exist in this world, and it is particularly through the creativity and audacity of youth that we can implement them in the epicentres of community: schools. Sometimes, it’s a bike event that nearly 200 people show up to, or a compost bin that accidentally became a garden over summer break, or a dusty shed that a shop class turned into a net-zero community hub. Across three schools in the Canadian provinces of Newfoundland & Labrador, Ontario, and Prince Edward Island, students have been building, growing, and pedalling their way toward a greener school and pulling their communities along for the ride. Most students at École St. Matthew’s in St. John’s, Newfoundland live within two kilometres of their school, yet most arrive by car anyway. The school set out to change that habit with its annual spring community event: Bikefest. Their annual community cycling Bikefest, held in May, drew 164 registered participants (double last year’s 82), plus walk-ins that pushed the total close to 200. Their local Member of Parliament and the provincial Minister of Education both attended, and 15 children were matched with refurbished bikes and scooters and given helmets through a re-CYCLING initiative the school plans to expand next year. Additionally, one of Canada’s most prominent youth climate action journals, The Starfish Canada , even interviewed and published a piece on the project a few months later. Behind the event is a longer project that has installed bike racks, a repair station, and solar lighting at the school, while hosting safety courses and family cycling days. Student lead Sawyer wrote letters to local businesses asking for helmet discounts and volunteer support, and he received more responses than the emails his teacher sent. The city is starting to notice, too! “The city’s starting to see that shared use pathways are an opportunity,” said teacher lead Mr. Shoemaker. “We can get people walking. We can get people more healthy.” This next project started during lockdown, when a group of friends attending Eden High School in Ontario discovered they liked plants. When school returned in person, they formed a greenhouse club, only to find their school’s greenhouse had sat unused for decades, overtaken by overgrown plants and falling into disrepair. They cleared it out, researched how to repair it, and got to work. A student at Eden High School tends to their plants in their school’s greenhouse. Photo courtesy of N:OW for Net-Zero . The greenhouse is now fully functional, sealed against winter heat loss and actively used by students learning sustainable agriculture. A composting program ran successfully alongside it until the compost bin spontaneously became a volunteer garden over the summer, which is honestly a great problem to have. More recently, the school received a Go Wild grant from WWF Canada to build a wildflower pollinator garden beside the greenhouse. What began as a club fixing a broken structure has grown into a broader ecological vision for the school. “In a way, this project has launched our school into somewhat of a larger eco project,” said teacher lead Mike Idzenga. A Grade 9 student put it simply: “With all the tips and tricks that I learned this year, for the rest of my life I can do that to plant my own garden.” Three Oaks High School doesn’t shy away from hosting events: sports games, races, community presentations. When they finally built a new outdoor sports field, it came with an awkward problem: it was far from the kitchen where food for events was prepared. The TOSH Cares Club and shop program decided to fix it by using the unused shed sitting on school property. Students gather at Three Oaks High School to retrofit their multipurpose outbuilding. Photo courtesy of N:OW for Net-Zero . Students across programs retrofitted the building, insulating it, wiring a solar system, and turning it into a net-zero multipurpose outbuilding that can now host classes, clubs, and events. Many TOSH Cares students had never taken shop before, and many shop students had never engaged with environmental education. The project brought them together, and both groups left changed. A sign on the shed now describes its net-zero impact to anyone who walks by. Gabby Cierra, a Grade 12 student, said something worth sitting with: “It kinda feels like we almost can’t make as much of an impact because we are not old enough to start big programs… but I think this is an example that we can.” All three of these schools came to N:OW for Net-Zero , a pan-Canadian student-led climate action program, with a real, tangible wish to improve their school grounds and, ultimately, enhance the living conditions of those attending and surrounding them. If this isn’t proof that climate action looks like whatever young people decide to make it, then we don’t know what is! The post The Many Ways Student-Led Climate Action Can Look appeared first on Happy Eco News .

Εγγραφείτε στο Reasons to be το εβδομαδιαίο ενημερωτικό δελτίο του Cheerful εδώ και θα λαμβάνετε το The Spark στα εισερχόμενά σας στην αρχή κάθε μήνα. Σε αυτό το τεύχος The power of communit…
items.descriptionOriginal: Welcome back to The Spark, our monthly celebration of how people just like you are creating positive change, one meaningful step at a time. The Spark is generously supported by Laura Rice. Sign up to Reasons to be Cheerful’s weekly newsletter here and you’ll get The Spark in your inbox at the start of each month. In this issue The power of community land trusts Cool roofs, cooler homes The perks of intergenerational roommates A community takes back its land In 2019, Nachand Trabue began noticing investors’ “We buy houses” signs all over her corner of Louisville, Kentucky. A historically Black neighborhood since the Civil War, Smoketown has deep roots and a long, proud past — including the city’s first Black library and first Black dentist, and as the birthplace of Muhammed Ali. But increasingly, long-term residents were getting priced out of their own community. For those like Trabue, a fourth-generation resident who remembered Smoketown in its thriving heyday, the change in their community was especially galling. “Because they’re taking away everything that made Smoketown great. They’re buying up the parks, the vacant lots, and putting in houses. There’s nothing for the kids. There’s no enrichment, no activity,” says Theresa Boyd, executive director of Smoketown Community Land Trust. A mural in Smoketown by The Art of Kacy. Credit: Don Sniegowski Trabue had had enough — she started pulling out the investors’ signs, reached out to the city’s land bank to figure out which vacant lots in the neighborhood were held by the city and connected with River City Housing , a local nonprofit home developer, to see how they could work together. At the same time, “the Smoketown Originals started to come together,” says Boyd, referring to a community organization of older residents with deep roots in the neighborhood. “They went to the churches, the community centers, the youth centers.” They started pushing the city to do a housing needs assessment and got in touch with Grounded Solutions , a national nonprofit for affordable housing, to decide whether a community land trust would be a viable option. Community land trusts (CLTs) are grassroots nonprofits that provide long-term affordable housing by buying and developing land on behalf of the community. When selling or renting homes, the CLT retains ownership of the land they’re built on, which makes the homes cheaper and keeps the land itself under community control. Crucially, CLTs also preserve affordability long-term by requiring owners to sell at an affordable price. The first CLTs grew out of the civil rights movement to secure land ownership for Black farmers. Today, they are an increasingly popular way of protecting land from speculators and creating long-term affordable housing, with over 300 CLTs in the US . The CLT’s first houses were recently completed, and more plots have already been chosen. Courtesy of Smoketown CLT In Smoketown, a lot of the initial work focused on explaining what a CLT is and getting the broader community on board. “Communities that have been divested [from] and have been talked to and at versus with, they lose their voice,” says Boyd. “We really had to rally the troops here in the community to be like, ‘You actually have a say in what goes on in your community.’” In 2020 the community and its partner organizations won the city’s Request for Proposals, securing $2.1 million to create a CLT. By 2023 the CLT was formalized and Boyd was brought onboard as the executive director. “I really whipped us into shape administratively and organizationally,” she says. “But most importantly, I went back out into the community and I was like, ‘Okay, this is what you wanted. Now what are we going to do with this land?’” Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] Based on a series of surveys, Smoketown CLT built its first seven houses right across the street from where Muhammed Ali threw his first punches under the watchful eye of trainer Fred Stoner, the grandfather of the CLT board president. These houses were recently completed, and the next seven plots have already been chosen. Before starting new developments, the CLT approaches the people living around the plots, says Boyd. “We invite them to the table: Okay, what are your concerns? What are your comments? This is what we are thinking. Is it a viable housing option for your street?” CLTs come in many different shapes, sizes and funding arrangements. In Smoketown, the CLT is funding the construction of the houses, but received the plots of land for free from the city. The land bank has earmarked around 70 plots in the neighborhood for the trust, says Boyd: “We were fortunate that those that came before me had enough gall to go to the city and be like, “Y’all holding all this land and you are absolutely not going to give it to investors. You are going to earmark it for the Community Land Trust.’ And we made them put it in writing.” Mayor Craig Greenberg joined Smoketown CLT to celebrate the completion of the CLT’s first seven homes. Courtesy of Smoketown CLT The city government has been supportive of the CLT, says Boyd, but it would not have happened without the community putting years of work into it. “Louisville’s been around for a really long time, and the people in our community absolutely will hold them to task, and that’s absolutely what they did. They started showing up at the council meetings, the reallocation of funds.” Partnering with experts, like Grounded Solutions, is key to getting a CLT off the ground, as is ensuring that community members see themselves represented in the CLT leadership, says Boyd. “[And] you have to be willing to change and really meet people where they are and not be afraid to make good trouble.” Learn more about Smoketown Community Land Trust here , or get additional information from Grounded Solutions here . Keeping it cool one roof at a time When Tony Chaves noticed how extreme heat and rising air-conditioning costs were affecting his Las Vegas neighborhood, he decided to help solve the problem with a ladder and a bucket of ultra-reflective white paint. As part of the two-person nonprofit Alchemical Opus, Chavez started painting the roofs of Arts District businesses for free, significantly decreasing their indoor temperatures, with one business owner reporting saving $60 to $70 a month on electricity. Coating roofs in white paint is an easy way to lower the temperatures of homes and public buildings. In recent years homeowners across India, Burkina Faso, Mexico and South Pacific have painted their roofs white as part of a global scientific study, with early results indicating substantial cooling. In the U.S., Philadelphia gave 62 households free cool-roof coatings in a 2025 pilot project, while the New York City CoolRoofs program has painted over 12 million square feet of roofs with reflective white paint since 2007. A number of U.S. cities also require cool roofs on new and re-roofed buildings. Wait, you're not a member yet? Join the Reasons to be Cheerful community by supporting our nonprofit publication and giving what you can. Join Cancel anytime The science behind the idea is straightforward: White and reflective roofs absorb less solar heat, and applying reflective coatings is the easiest way to transform a roof into a so-called “cool roof,” while also prolonging the life of the roof . The U.S. Department of Energy says cool roofs can reduce annual air-conditioning energy use in single-story buildings by up to 15 percent, while other studies show that painted roofs can lower maximum indoor temperatures by 2.2 to 5.9°F in residential buildings that are not air conditioned. Learn more about cool roofs here . Housing across generations After moving from the countryside to Vienna for university, Lukas Hecke, Manuel Schuler and Marlene Welzl experienced first-hand how difficult it could be to find good housing on a student budget. At the same time, they knew the city was full of elderly people with small pensions and large apartments, who often felt lonely after their children grew up and moved out. In 2015 they started connecting older people with spare rooms to younger people looking for a place to live. It began organically, by word of mouth, and soon grew into the housing platform Wohnbuddy that has carefully matched over 400 people based on their interests and communications over the years. The impact goes beyond private homes. Since 2017, Wohnbuddy has also partnered with senior residences, where students bring new energy through activities, music and social interaction. Learn more about Wohnbuddy here . The post The Spark: When Communities Own the Land, Housing Stays Affordable appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .
