items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Upcycling Food Industry Byproducts into Ingredients People Want to Eat Reading Time: 3 minutes Upcycling food industry byproducts turns factory leftovers into tasty, useful ingredients. Dutch company Greencovery shows how this can work for food makers. Upcycling food industry byproducts means turning leftover material from food factories into new ingredients. Food makers often call these leftovers side streams. Many side streams end up discarded or sold as animal feed. Greencovery , a company based in Wageningen in the Netherlands, wants to change that. It says its patented technology recovers valuable ingredients from side streams. The goal is to create new revenue for manufacturers and a lighter footprint on the planet. The scale of food waste is large. The UN Environment Programme reported that the world wasted 1.05 billion metric tons of food in 2022. That equals about 19% of the food available to consumers. Those figures cover homes, restaurants, and stores, not factory leftovers. Still, they show why finding new uses for food matters. Food loss and waste also affect the climate. The same report links it to 8% to 10% of global greenhouse gas emissions. That is almost five times the emissions from the aviation sector. A side stream is the material left after a factory makes its main product. That material often still holds useful compounds. Greencovery focuses on pulling those compounds out and returning them to the food supply. Animal feed is a common destination for these leftovers. Greencovery describes it as a lower-value outcome than human food. Its team sees upcycling food industry byproducts as a way to move more material toward food ingredients. The company uses what it calls mild separation technology. Separation means pulling the useful parts out of a mixture. Mild means gentle conditions, and the company says the method uses less energy and water than other separation techniques. Why does that matter? The company says the ingredients it extracts carry a low carbon footprint. A carbon footprint measures the greenhouse gases released to make a product. The recovered ingredients bring three listed strengths: high functionality, great taste, and microbial stability. Functionality means an ingredient performs well in recipes. Microbial stability means it resists spoilage by microbes and holds up in storage. Upcycling food industry byproducts turns okara, the often-overlooked soy pulp left after soy milk or tofu production, into Okara Pro and Okara Tex, two neutral-tasting, nutritious ingredients suited to bakery goods, savory dishes, and plant-based meat. Photo by Polina Tankilevitch on Pexels. Greencovery does not stop at the lab. It guides partners through three checkpoints for upcycling food industry byproducts. Each one answers a question. Does it work? Does the market want it? Is it commercially viable? The first checkpoint is a proof of concept, which tests whether the idea works technically. The team also runs early product trials to see if a side stream can become a functional ingredient. Next comes a proof of market, which checks whether buyers want the product. The team tests taste, function, and nutrition. It also brings potential buyers into the conversation early. The final step is a proof of business. It covers pricing, costs, profit margins, and supply chains. Greencovery also co-invests with partners and helps set up production in a suitable location. The team blends technology experts, food application specialists, and business experts. Together, they test both the science and the numbers. Two real products show upcycling food industry byproducts at work. The company has made a high-fiber satay sauce and a Parmigiano Reggiano mayonnaise. Both reflect its aim of using ingredients that might otherwise be discarded. The Dutch Prime Minister met the team and experienced both products firsthand. The meeting took place during the Netherlands’ food waste awareness week. Foodvalley NL, a group that promotes innovation and sustainability in food, invited Greencovery to the event. The talks focused on cutting food waste and finding better uses for ingredients. Greencovery also thanked the Upcycling Community for its support. Greencovery says it works to speed up the path from idea to market. Faster launches help companies see returns sooner. Manufacturers curious about their own side streams can start small. Greencovery offers a free 30-minute consultation call. These claims come from Greencovery itself, so readers should treat them as company-reported. Food makers considering upcycling their food byproducts should run their own trials and check local food safety rules before launching a product. Shoppers can play a part too. Choosing upcycled foods signals demand, which encourages more companies to try. Shoppers interested in upcycling food industry byproducts should read labels closely. A product can earn the upcycled label with only 10% upcycled ingredients by weight, so it helps to learn what the upcycled label actually requires. Organic foods, by comparison, must contain at least 95% certified organic ingredients. Food waste remains a large problem, but practical tools to shrink it are taking shape. Upcycling food industry byproducts gives manufacturers a clear path from leftover to ingredient. With testing, market checks, and careful planning, a side stream can become a product people choose to buy. The post Upcycling Food Industry Byproducts into Ingredients People Want to Eat appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Recommendations are independently selected by our team but may result in a commission to Nice News which helps keep our content free. Nice News readers know there’s no shortage of nice things in the world, and that includes products that make our lives a little better and brighter. In that spirit, we’re excited to share this roundup of our team’s favorite items from the past year — things we actually purchased (or received as gifts) and have loved using. For 2026, we’ve got an unbeatable hair brush, a cordless vacuum, scented bookmarks, and more. Combined, these 20 products comprise a pretty great holiday shopping guide, if we do say so ourselves. Scroll down for stocking stuffer ideas, big-ticket splurges, and practical presents that can be found in our team’s kitchens, closets, and makeup drawers. Ally, Staff Editor: Lykke Copper Interchangeable Knitting Needles Courtesy of Revolution Fibers Shop revolution fibers Shop Amazon This was my first “big” purchase after learning how to knit and getting a few projects under my belt. So far it’s been completely worth it — beyond looking beautiful, the copper needles offer the smoothness of stainless steel while conducting heat better, which I’ve read may make them easier on your joints (though there isn’t solid science to back that up). The set comes with every needle size a beginner could need, plus some interchangeable cords and a vegan suede case. Le Creuset Heritage Butter Dish Courtesy of Le Creuset Shop LE CREUSET Shop Amazon I received this adorable butter dish as a gift, and highly recommend giving it as one. It’s a relatively inexpensive way into the wide, wonderful world of Le Creuset ceramics and looks good in any kitchen. I have it in the deep yellow Nectar hue, but there are several other colors to choose from. Dyson Paddle Hairbrush Courtesy of Dyson Shop DYSON SHOP WALMART Dyson gets a lot of hype for its powerful blow dryers, but I’m here to sing the praises of the company’s humble hairbrush. items.descriptionOriginal: This article is part of The Optimist Daily’s Local Changemakers 2026 series, spotlighting changemakers 30 and under. Earlier this year, on a trip to Dominica to learn about the sperm whales that live in those Caribbean waters, Maya Higa was offered the chance to swim with them. She said no. Her reason was simple. “She would not participate in an activity that her followers would not be able to do,” wrote Maggie Kaplan, who nominated Maya for this series and was on the same trip. For most wildlife creators, that would have been the perfect moment for the cameras to come out. Maya turned on her livestream instead, talked with the boat crew and local staff about their work and lives, and shared the whales from her view on the surface. Kaplan came away moved by Maya’s resolve. “I was very impressed with her dedication on all fronts,” she wrote. But what she was describing wasn’t a sacrifice. It was consistency. Maya was doing exactly what she built Alveus Sanctuary to do. Building Alveus Maya founded Alveus in 2021 with a 21-hour charity stream on Twitch that raised more than $500,000. The platform came after the expertise, not the other way around. She grew up in Northern California and studied agricultural education and communication at Cal Poly San Luis Obispo. In college, she took a job as a zookeeper and completed internships at AZA-accredited facilities. She even got her falconry license. Part of the work involved going to schools and birthday parties to teach kids about animals in person, which gave her a taste for hands-on outreach and education. She went on to become a licensed wildlife rehabilitator. When she started streaming, all of that prior knowledge and experience came with her. What exactly is Alveus? Alveus is both a physical wildlife sanctuary in Austin, Texas, and a virtual education center. The sanctuary houses non-releasable animal ambassadors, which are animals that can’t survive in the wild but can represent their species and the ecosystems they come from. A 24/7 livestream on Twitch lets viewers watch them, get to know them by name, and connect with information about their wild counterparts. Other content creators can visit the sanctuary, run education programs, and extend the conservation message into communities Alveus wouldn’t otherwise reach. Conservation for a generation that grew up on Twitch The demographic Maya is reaching is one that traditional conservation organizations have struggled with for years. Maya “is reaching a whole new generation of 18 to 30 year olds through social media platforms that speak to their demographic,” Kaplan wrote. That generation didn’t grow up watching nature documentaries on television. They watch streams, follow creators, and decide what they care about based on communities they already belong to. “She is creating a new type of outreach,” Kaplan wrote, “a teaching platform about different species and their importance to our environment.” A teaching platform built around the creator-viewer relationship works differently from a broadcast. Viewers are compelled to come back. They recognize the individual animals. They get into discussions in the chat about things they’ve learned. Conservation education needs that kind of sustained attention, and with conventional methods, it doesn’t get it very often. Maya has over a million followers across her platforms, and those followers have made Alveus financially self-sustaining through their donations. Twitch donated $100,000 to the sanctuary directly. A partnership with WWF extended the work beyond the sanctuary itself. And Maya’s own TED talk, “ The wildlife sanctuary you can visit from anywhere ,” which she delivered in Vancouver, Canada, earlier this year, brought the model to an even broader professional audience. What comes next By 2026, Alveus has raised more than $7.5 million for conservation causes since its founding. The organization is actively expanding: new animal ambassadors coming in, enclosures being built out, and staff added to keep pace. Two projects are currently underway. The Pollinator Census is Alveus’s first community science initiative, where community members observe pollinator species in the sanctuary’s garden, and entomologists identify them, generating data to support insect conservation research. The greater effort is the Alveus Research and Recovery Institute (ARRI), developed in partnership with the Association of Zoos and Aquariums ‘ Saving Animals from Extinction (SAFE) program. ARRI’s first goal is a conservation breeding and release program for two critically endangered species: the Mexican Gray wolf and the Red wolf. It moves Alveus from education into direct intervention in species survival. The sperm whale moment in Dominica illustrates something about the whole operation. Maya went to Dominica to learn. When the choice came up, she ran the same calculation she’s always run: the point isn’t the experience she gets to have. It’s the one her audience gets to share with her. With a million people watching, that adds up to a different kind of reach than the field has seen. Learn more at bio.link/mayahiga . items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Two coral fragments fell over in a Stanford lab tank. When they touched, one healed the other. The bleached fragment, starved of the symbiotic algae that give coral both its color and its nutrition, began recovering within days. “We watched the healthy coral send over these colourful beneficial algae over to the bleached corals, and we watched its colour restore basically in front of our eyes,” said ocean scientist Danny Collins . Within a couple of weeks, the dying coral had recovered to the point where it was indistinguishable from its healthy neighbor. “We were blown away,” Collins said. “It does seem like this could open a door to possible reef restoration.” The findings , published last month in Science Advances , suggest that bleached coral is not necessarily dead, and that it can recover faster than researchers expected. The magic of the tissue bridge The recovery requires direct physical contact and a genetic match. When Collins’s team separated the fragments by a few millimeters, nothing happened. When they introduced corals from different genetic backgrounds, the corals rejected each other the way a body might reject a donated organ. When genetic clones made contact, their tissues fused. “They create a tissue bridge that kind of acts as a nutrient highway that allows for the healthy coral to then send over nutrients and this colourful algae over to the bleached coral,” Collins said. Coral is a colonial animal, a single organism made of thousands to millions of individual polyps. Fragments of the same genetic background recognize each other on contact and merge rather than fight. Collins noted this serves a natural function. If a piece breaks off in a wave, it can reconnect with the original colony. 96 percent of reefs are at risk The International Union for Conservation of Nature announced that about 96 percent of the world’s shallow-water reef systems are critically endangered and could disappear by 2075. Coral reefs support between a quarter and a third of all marine species, along with fisheries and coastal economies that hundreds of millions of people depend on. Coral scientist Julia Cole, who was not involved in the study, called the Stanford findings “a glimmer of light.” Cole chairs the Department of Earth and Environmental Sciences at the University of Michigan. She was enthusiastic but clear-eyed about scale. “If you think about the scale of reefs as kilometers, or in the case of the biggest reefs, thousands of kilometers … something that requires coral-to-coral contact, it would be a very meticulous and kind of overwhelming project,” she said. Collins’s team is working on extracting algae from healthy reefs, culturing it in labs, and deploying it to protect at-risk reefs ahead of expected bleaching events. “We hope in the near future we can have some interventions that actually could be field deployable and possibly scalable,” he said. The restoration work doesn’t address what’s warming the ocean in the first place. “We know how to solve the warming climate that’s causing these problems,” Cole said. “It comes back to getting serious about reducing greenhouse gas emissions, getting off of fossil fuels and transitioning to a clean-energy economy .” Source study: Science Advances – Rapid coral bleaching recovery via symbiont transfer from healthy corals Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . items.descriptionOriginal: Dietary guidelines seem to run the gamut depending on where you live. In Japan, grain-based dishes are the main focus, while Greece promotes the Mediterranean diet and the U.S. emphasizes protein . So nutrition scientists from around the globe recently came together to develop a compendium of advice that’s adaptable across cultures (and takes the health of the planet into account). Enter: the International Food Guide Pyramid. The team compared national and regional dietary guidelines from the United States, Canada, Germany, Australia, China, the Netherlands, and the Nordic countries, in addition to analyzing more than 250 scientific publications, to pinpoint the shared fundamentals of healthy eating. As it turns out, they may be more universal than it often seems. “Despite what people often hear, there’s actually substantial agreement in nutrition science about the foundations of healthy eating,” study lead Karen Della Corte said in a news release. She added that a balanced diet will look different for each person, so the guidelines are designed to be adjusted to include local, affordable, and culturally appropriate foods. The new food pyramid focuses on plant foods, healthier sources of fat and protein, and high-quality carbohydrates. At the base — representing the foundation of a nourishing diet — are vegetables and fruit as well as whole and low-glycemic index grains. Above that are plant-based proteins like beans, nuts, and seeds, as well as plant-based oils. Next up are fish, poultry, eggs, and certain dairy products, and at the top, for use sparingly, are refined grains, red and processed meats, butter, chips, sugary drinks and snacks, and salt. A 2025 report from the EAT-Lancet commission called for similarly plant-forward international guidelines, suggesting they could prevent 15 million premature deaths per year and reduce environmental impacts like greenhouse gas emissions. “Our diet has to be not only for our own health but also for the health of our planet,” said David Jenkins of the University of Toronto, creator of the glycemic index. “Our science base has to be appropriately comprehensive to include that.” Karen Della Corte Corte offered the following advice for putting the pyramid’s principles into practice: Design your meal around the plant food you want to emphasize, first thinking about which vegetables, whole grains, beans, or lentils you could include. Opt for beans, peas, lentils, fish, poultry, or yogurt more frequently than red or processed meats, and don’t make meat the biggest part of any meal. Reach for snacks like nuts, seeds, fruit, or vegetables with hummus over less nutritious processed options. Choose whole-grain bread over refined white bread and whole-grain or high-fiber cereals rather than refined, puffed, flaked, or popped cereals. Use canola or olive oil in your cooking instead of animal fats like butter or tallow. Drink water instead of soda.

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Endangered Animals Making a Comeback in 2027 Reading Time: 4 minutes Endangered Animals Making a Comeback in 2027 When you hear about endangered wildlife, it’s often another story of shrinking habitats, declining populations or species facing extinction. However, there is good news worth celebrating, too. Thanks to dedicated conservation efforts, some of the world’s most threatened animals are making remarkable comebacks. From mountain gorillas thriving in protected forests to bald eagles soaring across North America, you’ll find encouraging examples of how conservation can reverse population declines. Discover inspiring wildlife recovery stories that offer hope to endangered animals and show how your support for conservation can make a difference. 1. Mountain Gorillas Decades of habitat protection, veterinary care and anti-poaching initiatives have helped mountain gorilla populations grow to over 1,000 individuals , with multiple family groups. It’s a significant improvement for a species that once faced a much bleaker future. You’ll find these great apes in two isolated regions of Central and East Africa, where conservation teams work alongside local communities to protect the remaining habitat. The survival of this primate species extends beyond the gorillas themselves. Protecting large primates can also preserve entire ecosystems. While mountain gorillas remain endangered, their growing numbers demonstrate the value of long-term conservation. Expanding these efforts to other primate species may also protect smaller endangered species. 2. Bald Eagles Few wildlife recoveries are as impressive as that of the bald eagle. Once threatened by hunting, habitat destruction and the irresponsible use of the pesticide commonly known as DDT, America’s national bird has made an extraordinary species comeback. DDT led to poor-quality egg production, making successful breeding incredibly difficult for bald eagles. The ban on DDT, stronger legal protections and habitat conservation helped reverse decades of population decline. According to the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, the population in the lower 48 states increased from approximately 72,434 birds in 2009 to just over 316,000 birds , with 71,467 breeding pairs tracked between 2018 and 2019. Today, you’ll see bald eagles near rivers, lakes and coastlines across much of North America. Their remarkable recovery shows how environmental laws and sustained conservation efforts can give threatened wildlife a second chance. 3. Sea Turtles For sea turtles, the journey to adulthood begins with a dangerous dash from nest to ocean. Fortunately, conservation programs are giving more hatchlings a fighting chance through beach patrols, nest monitoring and community involvement. In the Philippines, conservationists have even recruited four-legged helpers. Project CURMA’s Paw Patrol uses specially trained dogs to sniff out buried turtle eggs , allowing volunteers to locate and protect nests from poachers and other threats. Efforts to reduce accidental catches in fishing nets, restore nesting beaches and limit artificial lighting along the coastlines are helping protect sea turtles at different stages of their lives. Some populations have shown encouraging improvements following decades of protection. While several sea turtle species remain endangered or critically endangered, initiatives like these show that creative conservation strategies can improve their chances of survival. When you participate in community initiatives, such as Paw Patrol, you increase the support that struggling species need to survive. 4. Tigers Tigers have lost much of their historical range to deforestation, human development and poaching. However, conservation efforts in parts of Asia are helping these magnificent predators reclaim lost ground. Wild tigers live across parts of Asia, where conservation efforts have helped some populations rebound after the global population fell to an estimated 3,200 in 2010. India offers one of the strongest examples, as it is now home to about 70% of the world’s wild tigers. Forest conservation has played a valuable part in this and other success stories. Sustainable forestry and other interventions have slowed global deforestation rates by almost 40% since the 1990s, which is why purchasing sustainably sourced timber is so important, whether you buy new floors, furniture or even musical instruments. Habitat loss remains a threat, but support for responsible forest management offers hope. 5. American Alligators American alligators were once hunted so extensively for their valuable skins that their survival became a serious concern. By 1967, the species had gained federal endangered status, prompting stronger protections against hunting and illegal trade. Conservation measures, including regulated harvesting and wetland management, helped restore their numbers. The species was removed from the U.S. endangered species list in 1987, just two decades after receiving protection. Today, up to 1.06 million mature American alligators inhabit the southeastern United States. With the species now classified as least concern, you’re looking at one of America’s most successful wildlife recovery stories. 6. Other Stories of Recovery The good news continues across the world. Other threatened species are showing encouraging signs of recovery, giving you even more reasons to feel hopeful about wildlife conservation. The Iberian lynx has rebounded from near extinction, thanks to captive breeding and habitat restoration across Spain and Portugal. North Atlantic right whales are also showing tentative signs of population growth, although their survival remains precarious. Meanwhile, giant pandas have benefited from decades of habitat protection and breeding programs, while southern white rhinos have recovered significantly from historical population lows through intensive conservation efforts. Humpback whales offer another success story, with several populations rebounding after commercial whaling restrictions gave these ocean giants a chance to recover. These achievements highlight the importance of patience and persistence, as rebuilding wildlife populations often requires decades of protection and ongoing monitoring. Every contribution makes a difference, and even keeping your distance from these animals, respecting protected habitats and choosing ethical wildlife tourism experiences contribute to various species’ success stories. Why Are More Endangered Animals Recovering? Wildlife recovery rarely happens by chance. Behind these success stories are years of coordinated conservation efforts, scientific research and communities working to protect vulnerable species. These efforts also benefit entire ecosystems. When you protect forests, wetlands and oceans, you’re helping preserve the habitats that countless species depend on for survival. Several approaches are helping endangered animals rebuild their populations: Habitat protection: National parks, wildlife corridors and sustainable land management give animals safer places to live, breed and find food. Stronger wildlife laws: Hunting restrictions, anti-poaching patrols and international trade regulations help reduce human-driven threats. Breeding and reintroduction programs: Conservationists can raise threatened animals in protected environments and then release them into suitable habitats where they have a better chance of thriving. Community involvement: Local conservation projects encourage people to protect wildlife while supporting livelihoods through responsible tourism and sustainable practices. Scientific monitoring: Tools like GPS collars, population surveys, and genetic research help conservationists spot problems earlier and celebrate progress when recovery efforts work. A Brighter Future for Endangered Wildlife Every species making a comeback represents years of dedication and a reminder that extinction isn’t always inevitable. Although many endangered animals still face serious threats, these conservation successes show that meaningful progress is possible. You can help sustain that momentum by supporting wildlife conservation organizations, choosing responsibly sourced products and spreading awareness about threatened species. Even small actions contribute to a broader movement to protect biodiversity. With continued commitment, today’s recovery stories could become tomorrow’s thriving wildlife populations. The post Endangered Animals Making a Comeback in 2027 appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: A former Los Angeles gang member, a former skinhead and a former radical Islamist walk into a youth center. What sounds like the setup for an uneasy joke is at the core of Farah Pandith’s work: Put people who might otherwise never share a room in front of young people; let them explain what drew them into extremism and how they found their way out. “They’re the most authentic and credible voices there are,” Pandith says. More than once she has observed that their stories reach an audience that official warnings cannot. For decades, including while working for the U.S. government under the Obama, George W. Bush and George H.W. Bush administrations, Pandith researched why people embrace ideologies that divide the world into “us versus them.” Before people can be persuaded away from hatred, she argues, one has to understand what they are looking for: recognition, certainty or a place in the world. “You don’t suddenly explode and become an extremist overnight. You’re having some self-doubt, you’re asking questions about who you are,” she says from her light-filled living room in Arlington, Virginia. Preventing someone from becoming an extremist has been her lifelong goal, because it’s “infinitely easier than dealing with the fallout.” Farah Pandith visits the Indonesian city of Bekasi during her time as the U.S. special representative to Muslim communities. Credit: U.S. Embassy, Jakarta / Wikimedia Commons While working for the government, she traveled to nearly 100 countries, from Belgium to Bangladesh, to understand how extremists’ descent into violence can be interrupted. Today she applies what she learned to a broader problem: how to make compassion more than an admirable sentiment and help communities put it into practice. Last year Pandith received the ADL Daniel Pearl Award , which is given annually to a person who has had a positive impact on understanding between Jews and the Muslim world, and is sponsored by the parents of the journalist who was kidnapped and killed in Pakistan in 2002. “It is hard to think of anyone more knowledgeable than Farah Pandith when it comes to countering violent extremism,” Joseph Nye, the late chair of the National Intelligence Council, said about her. On September 11, 2001, Pandith watched on television like millions of others as two planes struck the World Trade Center. “It felt very heavy,” she recalls, putting a hand to her heart. “The world kind of went still for a moment, like, ‘What do we do about this?’” She felt compelled to act, to help prevent such violence from happening again. She especially rejected the way extremists attempted to define her religion on the airwaves. “Who are they to dictate what Islam is?” she remembers thinking. “For me, Islam means humility, compassion, to treat others with respect.” Initially, when she worked for the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID), cooperating with local organizations showed her that effective policy depends on understanding the people on the ground. “You have to listen really well to find a solution that matches with the local community,” she says. “That’s tricky and complex. Trust has to be built first.” The same principle, she realized, applied to preventing violent extremism. Government officials could not design effective strategies from Washington alone. They needed to hear from the people they hoped to reach, including those whose voices had been overlooked. After joining the National Security Council in 2004, Pandith helped develop the “soft power” side of the Global War on Terror through a new approach called Countering Violent Extremism. Military action might disrupt extremist organizations, but it could not prevent them from recruiting new members. Nor were public relations campaigns successful in overcoming the distrust of Muslims worldwide. Even in her own government, distrust was impossible to ignore. One congressman called the White House to complain a “jihadist” was sitting in the Council. Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] Pandith was briefly living in Afghanistan’s capital, Kabul, in 2004 when photographs of abuse at Abu Ghraib surfaced showing American soldiers humiliating Muslim prisoners. “In an instant, all our efforts on the ground were harmed irreparably,” she says. Locals asked how she could represent a government that treated Muslim prisoners that way. The experience reinforced a lesson: Building trust also meant receiving criticism, sitting through uncomfortable conversations. Pandith carried that approach into her work at the State Department, where Hillary Clinton appointed her the first U.S. special representative to Muslim communities in 2009. Instead of treating Muslim populations as a single audience for American messages, she traveled widely, meeting people in homes, mosques and community settings to learn what mattered to them. “You have to go to the rural areas,” she says, aiming to support credible local voices that could offer alternatives to extremist narratives. Pandith herself has been shaped by a background that made her an ideal diplomat. She came to the U.S. from Kashmir as a baby with her mother, a pulmonologist and the medical director of a hospital. Pandith describes growing up in a highly educated Muslim family without experiencing discrimination. She remembers an America in which people of different faiths could live alongside one another, “with a synagogue, a church, a mosque and a temple in the same part of town.” Today, she admits, that harmonious coexistence feels nearly impossible. Her parents separated when she was 10, and her mother raised Pandith and her brother on her own. One of her greatest influences was her uncle, a heart surgeon. “I’ve held the hearts of different people in my hands,” he would tell her. “Always remember: There is no difference between the heart of a Muslim, a Jew, a Hindu or a Christian.” Pandith feels she carries “many identities” — an American, a woman, a Muslim and a foreign policy professional, among others. While traveling as Special Representative to Muslim Communities in the Obama administration, she said she had a “superpower” when speaking with Muslims. When she told them she was born in Srinagar in Kashmir, India, the atmosphere often changed. “Suddenly I’m like a sister to them.” Farah Pandith on a panel at the Milken Institute Asia Summit. Courtesy of Farah Pandith Her ability to forge connections would become one of her greatest professional assets. By chance, Barbara Bush, the wife of President George H.W. Bush, visited Smith College during Farah’s senior year. She was so impressed by a speech Pandith gave as student body president that she helped her secure her job at USAID after graduation. That was how the young woman began traveling around the world. Pandith’s work challenged conventional explanations of radicalization. Poverty and lack of education, she argued, could not explain why people embraced violent ideologies. Some of the 9/11 terrorists were well educated. Pandith pointed to a different cause she observed in Muslim communities: deep identity crises among young people who struggled to find their place in a rapidly changing world. She thinks of a young woman in Denmark whose Imam told her she wasn’t a Muslim if she didn’t cover her head. Or Mubin Shaikh in Canada, who went to Pakistan and Syria as a 19-year-old to fight alongside the jihadists and who now teaches security politics at the University of Ottawa. Pandith has seen firsthand that dialogue can change minds. ““It’s less interesting for the media than an extremist’s video, but the conversations we had affected people.” Her initiatives have sought to make dialogue a shared responsibility. Against Violent Extremism became the world’s first and only network of former extremists, launched by the U.S. Department of State, the Institute for Strategic Dialogue and Google. The “Hours Against Hate” campaign encouraged teenagers to spend an hour doing something for someone different from themselves. Millions participated. Sisters Against Violent Extremism connected mothers concerned about their children’s vulnerability to extremist recruitment. In a citizen-dialogue program, Pandith traveled through Europe with other Muslim Americans to share experiences and listen to local concerns. People had the chance to meet someone they might otherwise see only through stereotypes and to develop a relationship that complicated those assumptions. In her book How We Win , recently reissued, Pandith remains stubbornly optimistic: The fight against extremism can be won. Preventing people from being drawn into extremist movements requires intervening early and bringing together the people who can reach them — not just government officials, but business leaders, teachers, local communities and influencers whose networks, knowledge and credibility government agencies lack. “The fight against violent extremism is not going to be won solely by the efforts of government,” she argues. “We need businesses to step up as never before, for the public interest as well as their own.” She insists that this work cannot be dismissed as idealism or do-goodery but is “a matter of national security” — as important as the hard power of military force. Pandith emphasizes that the underlying lessons can be relevant for many communities. The same dynamics of exclusion and dehumanization can fuel hostility toward religious minorities, LGBTQ+ people and Asian communities, among others. Still, she admits that the strategies for countering violent extremism never fully came to fruition, often mired in bureaucracy. “Congress provided just 0.0138 percent of funding compared to the funding for the military,” she calculates. “We know what we need to do. We spent 25 years researching and exchanging strategies. But we left the field to the extremists.” Pandith sees the reality as a call to action: “We cannot just wring our hands and keep saying things are bad and things are difficult and somebody else’s problem. We need everybody.” Wait, you're not a member yet? Join the Reasons to be Cheerful community by supporting our nonprofit publication and giving what you can. Join Cancel anytime She now works outside government to advance another part of this agenda, as senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations , teaching countering violent extremism at Georgetown University, and as a Global Peace Laureate for the Muhammad Ali Center. She has been developing the Muhammad Ali Index on compassion . For Pandith, compassion is the capacity to recognize another person’s humanity even amid disagreement, and to resist the impulse to turn differences into a reason for contempt. “There isn’t a faith on planet Earth that doesn’t have compassion in it. And even if you are not religious you understand what it means, right?” As part of the Muhammed Ali Index, more than 5,400 people in 12 American cities responded to the 2025 State of Compassion survey . Sixty-one percent said they felt compassion has declined in the last four years, but 43 percent were optimistic about the future of compassion in America. A second index, planned for 2027, will cover 20 U.S. cities and 12 cities around the world. The ambition is practical. Pandith hopes the data will help mayors, school leaders, faith groups and local organizations identify opportunities to build stronger connections and design efforts suited to their own communities. The point is not to prescribe a universal program, but to create a framework that can be adapted. “We want to see people taking inspiration from the data to actually do something over time so we can measure and see what takes place,” she says passionately, insisting that compassion can be trained: “Compassion is a muscle that can be exercised.” Yet the starting point is personal: “Self-compassion is essential.” Building the capacity for compassion, Pandith argues, begins with recognizing what is happening inside oneself. She is particularly interested in reaching young people early. “The world that they are growing up in is so polarized and so difficult and so different from the one that we have grown up in,” she says, “that they don’t have a memory of people who are different from them speaking to each other with dignity regularly.” As Pandith sees it, waiting for polarization to disappear on its own is not a strategy. The task is to build relationships and connections that open up hearts and minds — and to keep investing in them long enough to learn what works. She repeats her favorite sentence: “Solutions are available and affordable.” UPDATE — November 3, 2026: This story has been updated to clarify facts about Pandith’s work and background. The post The Counter-Extremism Expert Building Our Capacity for Compassion appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .

items.descriptionOriginal: Some bees line their nests with soft petals. Some line them with hardened tree sap. Some line them with a thin, flexible film composed of silk and polyester. And this latter group—known as cellophane bees—may hold the key to sustainable, biodegradable plastic, according to a new study. “Nature has already solved a problem that polymer scientists are still working on: a bioplastic that is chemically and physically similar to conventional plastics but doesn’t persist in the environment,” says study team member Jonathan Coote , assistant professor in the Department of Sustainable Biomaterials at Virginia Tech University. Unlike more familiar hive-dwelling honeybees, cellophane bees nest in the soil. Females lay eggs in individual chambers that they line with secretions from a gland on their abdomen. Scientists have known for almost half a century that this lining is composed of silk fibers and a polyester similar to polyethylene—a material that makes up about one-third of human-produced plastics and is the most commonly used plastic for packaging. “Polyethylene-like polyesters made in the lab generally don’t break down well in the environment,” says Coote. “The bees’ material, however, breaks down rapidly in soil.” Although the bees nest in aggregations of 10,000 or more individual nests and often use the same nest sites for decades, their habitat never becomes choked with plastic—in contrast to large aggregations of modern humans. To find out more about how the bees do it, Coote and his collaborators gathered nest linings from two Tennessee nest sites of a species of cellophane bee known as Colletes inaequalis . They put the material through a battery of tests to characterize its structure and chemical makeup. They also collected nest linings that had been in the ground for four, seven, and 11 months to track how the material degrades over time. .IRPP_ruby , .IRPP_ruby .postImageUrl , .IRPP_ruby both;} Recommended Reading: There’s no such thing as a free polymer. The tradeoff at the heart of bioplastics. A fresh nest cell lining is about 73% polyester and 27% silk by weight, the researchers report. The polyester is semicrystalline, likely has cross-linked polymer chains, and has a crystal structure and degradation temperature similar to that of polyethylene. “The biggest surprise was that the material is most likely cross-linked, meaning its polymer chains are chemically tied together into a network,” says Coote. “Cross-linked plastics, called thermosets, are typically very durable, and designing thermosets that break down at the end of their life is a major challenge in polymer science. So finding a thermoset that breaks down rapidly in soil was very counterintuitive, and it’s exciting to have a natural example to learn from.” By four months, the nest linings are just 40% polyester, meaning that the polyester degrades even more rapidly than famously biodegradable silk in the first months (after that, the composition changes much more slowly). Four-month-old nest linings remain flexible and intact, protecting the nest cell from moisture and microbes like a shrink-wrapped bell pepper at the grocery store. By seven months, about the time the larva has developed into an adult bee, the lining easily cracks easily; by 11 months, it crumbles in the hand. In other words, unlike that bell pepper’s shrink wrap, the nest lining lasts just as long as is needed to protect the developing bee, and no longer. The researchers next aim to investigate how the material breaks down so quickly. They hypothesize that the particularities of polyester’s crystal structure may leave the bonds that connect the material’s subunits exposed to a greater degree than in other polyesters. There’s also evidence of an enzyme that breaks these bonds present in the nest lining, perhaps from the mother bee’s saliva. “The goal is to reverse engineer what the bees are doing so that we can design similar materials in the lab and eventually produce them at practical scale,” Coote says. Source: Coote J.P., et al. “ Rapid soil degradation of a cross-linked, semicrystalline polyethylene-like polyester produced by Colletes bees .” PNAS 2026. Image: Laura Russo.

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News How Wildlife Conservation Filmmaking Turns Powerful Stories into Real-World Action Reading Time: 3 minutes Wildlife conservation filmmaking connects audiences with wild places and the people protecting them. Wildlife conservation filmmaking gives viewers a reason to care about wild places they may never see in person. Fin and Fur Films , an award-winning production company, builds its work around that idea. Its team focuses on wildlife, adventure, and conservation stories. The company says it is proudest of films that led to real-world conservation impacts. That goal shapes every project. In wildlife conservation filmmaking, a film succeeds when it moves audiences to care, not just when it entertains. Ben Masters, founder and director, started the company in 2012 with a Kickstarter campaign. Kickstarter is an online fundraising platform where many people donate small amounts. That campaign paid for the film Unbranded. Unbranded follows four young cowboys who adopted, trained, and rode a string of wild mustangs 3,000 miles from Mexico to Canada. That is about the distance across the continental United States. The route crossed some of the wildest terrain in the American West. The trip included runaway horses, a sassy donkey, perilous mountain passes, and rodeos. It also brought sickness, injury, and death. The film won the Audience Award at Telluride Mountainfilm and the Hot Docs Film Festival. Unbranded also shines a light on the complex situation facing the country’s wild horses. The adventure holds attention, and the film explains the issue along the way. Wildlife conservation filmmaking often works this way. The River and the Wall takes a similar approach. Five friends travel 1,200 miles from El Paso to the Gulf of Mexico through the unknown wilds of the Texas borderlands. They go by horse, mountain bike, and canoe. That distance equals nearly a full day of nonstop highway driving, but the friends covered it much more slowly. They set out to document the borderlands. They also wanted to explore how a border wall could affect the natural environment. As the wilderness gave way to the more populated Lower Rio Grande Valley, the friends met the human side of the immigration debate. The trip took an emotional turn they had not planned for. Deep in the Heart: A Texas Wildlife Story brings wildlife conservation filmmaking to an entire state. Actor Matthew McConaughey narrates the visually stunning film. It celebrates Texas landscapes and wildlife found nowhere else. Wildlife conservation filmmaking comes to an entire state in Deep in the Heart: A Texas Wildlife Story , narrated by Matthew McConaughey, a visually stunning film celebrating Texas landscapes and wildlife found nowhere else. Photo courtesy of Fin and Fur Films . The film aims to protect the state’s remaining wild places. It shows how water and wildlife depend on each other. It also recognizes Texas’s important role in conservation across the continent. Reach matters in wildlife conservation filmmaking. Fin and Fur Films has shared its work through Netflix, Apple TV, PBS Nature, Prime, National Geographic, and LoveNature. The films have also appeared in large theatrical releases and on international television. Global Wildlife Conservation notes that well-made environmental documentaries can bring people closer to nature and inspire them to protect it. The Fin and Fur Films catalog shows how that works in practice. Each story pairs a real adventure with a real conservation question. Partnerships help wildlife conservation filmmaking go further. The company has worked with American Rivers, The Nature Conservancy, and Texan by Nature. It has also partnered with brands such as H-E-B and YETI. The numbers show how far a small team can stretch. The company has produced five feature films and more than 30 short films. It has worked with more than 40 conservation groups, which is roughly one partner group per film. See also: A Documentary About Overfishing Sparked Blue Marine Foundation’s Ocean Conservation Mission Masters says the crew keeps its roots as river lovers, backcountry horsemen, and field-savvy wildlife biologists. He also stresses that each film is a team effort. Dozens, or even hundreds, of people contribute to each one. Masters credits partners, collaborators, donors, contractors, and the viewers who give their time to watch. That shared support keeps the work going. Audiences are part of the effort, too. Good stories make conservation feel personal. Wildlife conservation filmmaking gives those stories a wide audience. Which wild place would you most like to see protected next? The post How Wildlife Conservation Filmmaking Turns Powerful Stories into Real-World Action appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Goldman Prize Honors Young Activist for Stopping Fracking in Colombia’s Magdalena River Towns Reading Time: 3 minutes Yuvelis Morales Blanco won the 2026 Goldman Environmental Prize for stopping fracking in Colombia’s Magdalena River communities and helping halt two pilot projects and secure a landmark court ruling. A university student began stopping fracking in Colombia’s Magdalena River towns by knocking on her neighbors’ doors. Seven years later, Yuvelis Morales Blanco has won the 2026 Goldman Environmental Prize for that work. The prize honors grassroots environmental leaders from six world regions each year. Her campaign helped stop two pilot fracking projects near her hometown of Puerto Wilches. It also led to a Constitutional Court ruling that upheld her Afro-Colombian community’s right to a say. To date, no fracking project has moved forward anywhere in Colombia. Morales Blanco, now 24, grew up in a family of subsistence fishers on the Magdalena River. The river flows nearly 1,000 miles from the Andes to the Caribbean, about the distance from Boston to Atlanta. For the roughly 30,000 people of Puerto Wilches, it provides food, income, and identity. The town also sits in the heart of Colombia’s oil country. Ecopetrol, the largest and majority state-owned oil company, is based in nearby Barrancabermeja. Between 2015 and 2022, about 40% of its more than 2,000 oil spills happened in this region. That works out to roughly two spills a week for eight years. In 2018, a leak at the Lizama 158 well displaced about 100 families and killed thousands of fish. So when the government proposed fracking nearby, residents had reason to worry. In 2019, then-President Iván Duque announced two pilot projects called Kalé and Platero. Ecopetrol led both, with ExxonMobil as operator and majority partner on Platero. Fracking, short for hydraulic fracturing, pumps water, sand, and chemicals into rock at high pressure. The pressure cracks the rock and frees trapped oil or gas. The process uses large amounts of water and can contaminate rivers and groundwater. Morales Blanco was studying environmental engineering at the time. She paused her degree and began visiting neighbors to explain the risks. She also joined the Alianza Colombia Libre de Fracking, or Colombia Free from Fracking Alliance. With the alliance, she helped lead protests outside the Ecopetrol refinery. In January 2022, she testified at permit hearings and organized a peaceful sit-in. Soon after the sit-in, armed men showed up at her home. She fled Colombia, and France granted her asylum in February 2022. No one has been convicted for the threats against her. Exile in France did not end her campaign. She received the Marianne Initiative award for human rights defenders and raised the issue with President Emmanuel Macron. She also brought the case before the International Rights of Nature Tribunal. Back home, the campaign for stopping fracking in Colombia’s Magdalena River towns began winning in court. In April 2022, a court suspended environmental permits for both projects until companies consulted local communities. Months later, newly elected President Gustavo Petro announced his opposition to fracking. Community organizing helped secure a court-ordered suspension of two fracking projects in 2022, a key step in stopping fracking in Colombia’s Magdalena River, followed months later by President Gustavo Petro’s opposition to fracking. Photo by Christian Escobar Mora courtesy of Goldman Environmental Prize . Ecopetrol suspended the project contracts in September 2022. By November, it had halted Kalé and Platero and undone its agreements with ExxonMobil. The decisive ruling came in August 2024. Colombia’s Constitutional Court found that the pilots violated the community’s right to free, prior, and informed consent. Under this principle, companies must consult communities and win their agreement before projects affect their land. That decision reaches beyond Puerto Wilches. It confirms that Afro-Colombian communities have a legal voice over what happens on their territory. The precedent matters for stopping fracking in Colombia’s Magdalena River communities and anywhere similar projects appear. Morales Blanco has since returned to Puerto Wilches and keeps organizing with the alliance. She describes the Magdalena as the life that sustains her family and her fishing community. She also points out that her region produces great energy wealth while many residents stay poor. The Global Greengrants Fund, which supports the alliance, notes that each prize winner represents a broader movement. More than 80 of the fund’s partners and allies have received the prize since 1993. Afro-Colombian fishing communities stood beside her in stopping fracking in Colombia’s Magdalena River towns. Morales Blanco won for the South and Central America region, one of six 2026 winners , all of whom were women. The others came from Nigeria, South Korea, the United Kingdom, Papua New Guinea, and the United States. Colombia’s politics have shifted since her win. President Abelardo de la Espriella took office in August 2026 after campaigning to expand fracking. Still, the 2024 ruling gives communities like Puerto Wilches firm legal ground to demand a say. Stopping fracking in Colombia’s Magdalena River communities didn’t require a big budget or political office. It took a young woman who knew her river and kept going after threats forced her abroad. Her prize shows how local action can shape national policy. The post Goldman Prize Honors Young Activist for Stopping Fracking in Colombia’s Magdalena River Towns appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: A small knitted tube — open at both ends, just wide enough for two hands — and a child with anxiety found each other in an Austrian classroom. That quiet moment is at the heart of Ursula Kermer's decade-long project, Mehr ist Mehr ("More is More"), a volunteer network that turns individual squares of yarn into blankets, boleros, and twiddle muffs for people moving through hard seasons of life. Kermer, an art therapist, is honest about what the project cannot do: "Our project does not solve problems; it does not make crisis go away." But it is constant, and that constancy — the weekly knitting circles, the puzzling together of mismatched squares, the packages of wool arriving unbidden from strangers — turns out to be its own kind of medicine. The blankets travel to families whose children have cancer, to people who cannot pay their heating bills, to rehabilitation centers where a counselor leaves them draped over chairs so that someone in crisis might simply reach out and choose one. Most knitters never know whose hands will eventually hold their work, and Kermer photographs every step so they know where it ends — just not with whom. She describes the whole endeavor as resilience training in disguise: choosing a color, trusting a process, watching mismatched pieces become something whole. For her, the image that holds it all is a network — "growing and moving, and provides a resilient safety" — as easily overlooked, but just as strong as the individual threads that compose spools of yarn.

items.description: Happy Eco News Οι Cofán Rangers προστατεύουν τη φρουρά του Αμαζονίου 450.000 εκτάρια τροπικού δάσους του Ισημερινού Χρόνος ανάγνωσης: 3 λεπτά Οι δασοφύλακες της Cofán που προστατεύουν τον Αμαζόνιο μεταφέρουν δέματα 100 λιβρών σε περιπολίες διάρκειας μηνών, υπερασπίζοντας την περιοχή των προγονικών τροπικών δασών που ωφελεί ολόκληρο τον πλανήτη. Οι δασοφύλακες της Cofán που προστατεύουν τον Αμαζόνιο έχουν διαφυλάξει τον Εκουαδόρ…
items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Cofán Rangers Protecting the Amazon Guard 450,000 Hectares of Ecuadorian Rainforest Reading Time: 3 minutes Cofán rangers protecting the Amazon carry 100-pound packs on monthlong patrols, defending ancestral rainforest territory that benefits the entire planet. The Cofán rangers protecting the Amazon have safeguarded the Ecuadorian rainforest for centuries, living where the Amazon Basin rises toward the Andes. Among the region’s oldest surviving indigenous cultures, the Cofán now protect more than one million acres of ancestral territory, roughly the size of the U.S. state of Delaware, containing primary forest, wild rivers, swamplands, and several thousand plant and animal species found nowhere else. That protection intensified after oil exploitation and the colonists who followed threatened to overwhelm Cofán lands. In response, Cofán leadership founded Fundación Sobrevivencia Cofán in 1999, an organization built on what its founders described as a fight-for-rights-or-disappear mindset. The Cofán Survival Fund, an independent U.S.-based nonprofit, supports that work by channeling donations directly into Cofán-led conservation programs. At the center of Cofán people’s protection of the Amazon is GuardAmazonas Cofán, formerly known as the Cofán Park Guards. Since 2003, teams of Cofán rangers have delimited, secured, monitored, and protected their homeland, using GPS units and drones to gather intelligence on threats before coordinating with police and the military to counter illegal incursions. The program’s success convinced Ecuador’s Ministry of Environment to more than double the Cofán’s legally recognized ancestral territory. Today, nearly 50 Cofán rangers patrol in five-person teams, carrying full packs on monthlong expeditions that demand extreme physical fitness and deep forest knowledge. Unlike many indigenous territory-protection programs, GuardAmazonas pays its rangers, recognizing that sustained, full-time conservation work demands fair compensation for families bearing real costs and risks. Teams deliberately mix members from different communities and generations, transmitting ecological knowledge across the Cofán homeland while strengthening unified national identity. Cofán rangers protecting the Amazon through GuardAmazonas receive fair pay for sustained, full-time conservation work, with patrol teams deliberately mixing members from different communities and generations to transmit ecological knowledge across the Cofán homeland. Photo courtesy of Cofán Survival Fund . The work of Cofán rangers protecting the Amazon extends well beyond ranger patrols into cultural survival and scientific partnership. Between 2001 and 2008, the foundation coordinated four Rapid Biological Inventories with Chicago Field Museum biologists, leading directly to expanded territorial protection. That collaboration earned a 2013 MacArthur Award for Creative and Effective Institutions. The Charapa Project shows how Cofán rangers protecting the Amazon lead species recovery. Commercial egg harvesting nearly eliminated the Amazonian river turtle from Ecuadorian beaches until Cofán communities began raising hatchlings in protected ponds in the 1980s, dramatically improving survival rates before release. In Zábalo, families now protect most turtle nests they find, and travelers along the Aguarico River encounter river turtles sunning themselves on nearly every log once they enter Cofán territory, a result confirmed by peer-reviewed research co-authored by Cofán community members. Climate change has not spared Cofán lands, prompting the creation of the Lifeboat Garden Project. As scorching temperatures and unpredictable rainfall diminished important food and medicinal plant species, project leaders transplanted them to more ecologically stable upriver land, preserving botanical knowledge for future generations while protecting additional forest in a heavily deforested area. Cofán rangers protecting the Amazon also invest in human capital. The Cofán Higher Education Project sends entire families, not just individual students, to Quito, where parents pursue university degrees while children attend quality schools, preserving language and cultural identity through shared communal housing. The Seguro Campesino Project enrolls Cofán families in Ecuadorian social welfare programs, sends medical brigades to remote communities, and removes financial pressures that might otherwise force compromises on territorial conservation commitments. Innovation among Cofán rangers protecting the Amazon also extends to transportation. After the successful Ecocanoa Project taught Cofán artisans to build durable fiberglass canoes instead of felling endangered trees, the Solar Canoe Project now develops battery-powered alternatives to fossil-fuel motors, creating quieter waterways that benefit wildlife, hunting, fishing, and ecotourism alike. Ecotourism remains central to Cofán rangers protecting the Amazon, tracing back to the 1970s, when FSC founder Randy Borman and Cofán community members began hosting visitors along the Aguarico River and eventually established the community of Zábalo. Rather than staging performances, Cofán guides position themselves as credentialed experts who share ecological knowledge directly, keeping more revenue by controlling ecotourism operations rather than losing profits to outside intermediaries. Felipe Borman, current Executive Director of the foundation and recently elected Director of Territory for the Cofán ethnic federation NOA’IKE, continues work his father Randy began, coordinating fieldwork across the Cofán-Bermejo Ecological Reserve and Río Cofanes Territory. The foundation’s Rapid Response Team stays vigilant over changing laws and policies that threaten Cofán land rights, while accompanying patients through Ecuador’s healthcare system and coordinating visits from scientists, officials, and allies. As climate negotiations worldwide increasingly recognize indigenous stewardship as essential to global conservation outcomes, Cofán rangers protecting the Amazon demonstrate what sustained, community-led territorial defense can achieve. The foundation emphasizes that funding Cofán rangers protects the forest the whole world depends on, not just Cofán communities, positioning indigenous-led conservation as climate infrastructure that benefits everyone far beyond Ecuador’s Amazonian lowlands. The post Cofán Rangers Protecting the Amazon Guard 450,000 Hectares of Ecuadorian Rainforest appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.titleOriginal: Tiny Backpacks Reveal the Secret, Sometimes Circuitous Migrations of Small Songbirds
items.description: Αυτό το άρθρο γράφτηκε από τη Stephanie Szarmach, μεταδιδακτορικό συνεργάτη James Smithson στο Smithsonian Institution, για το The Conversation — έναν μη κερδοσκοπικό ειδησεογραφικό οργανισμό αφιερωμένο στην ανταλλαγή γνώσεων ερευνητών και επιστημόνων, με άδεια Creative Commons. Διαβάστε το πρωτότυπο άρθρο εδώ. Στραβίζοντας μέσα από τα κιάλια μου, σάρωση th…
items.descriptionOriginal: This article was written by Stephanie Szarmach , a James Smithson Postdoctoral Fellow at the Smithsonian Institution, for The Conversation — a nonprofit news organization dedicated to sharing the knowledge of researchers and scientists, under a Creative Commons license . Read the original article here . Squinting through my binoculars, I scanned the dense branches of a black spruce, trying my best to catch a glimpse of the thin legs of a small black, white, and yellow songbird. I was on the hunt for a yellow-rumped warbler — a bird affectionately called “butter-butt” by bird-watchers after the distinctive buttery yellow patch of feathers above its tail. Once I spotted a flash of red on one of the bird’s legs, I knew that this individual was special — in fact, it was one that I already knew well. That’s because I had placed identifying bands on it the previous year as part of my Ph.D. research , and it was carrying a very important piece of new technology. Johanna Beam Stephanie Szarmach holds a yellow-rumped warbler that was banded as part of a study. I played the high-pitched “warble ” of its song through a speaker placed below a mist net of fine, nearly invisible mesh. Thinking another male had intruded on his territory, the bird quickly descended. My tactic worked — he got caught in the net. As I gently removed him, I breathed a sigh of relief as I saw the Tic Tac-size device sitting on his back. Over the past year, this warbler carried a multisensor geolocator backpack throughout his migratory journey, recording the long trek from his breeding grounds in Anchorage, Alaska, to a yet unknown winter refuge and back again. Working with my Ph.D. adviser, evolutionary biologist David Toews , I deployed dozens of these cutting-edge tags to illuminate the migratory journeys of these high-latitude breeding warblers at a scale not previously possible for small birds. Stephanie Szarmach A yellow-rumped warbler wears a multisensor geolocator backpack. Now, after a year of waiting, I finally had the data in hand. How Can Scientists Track Small Birds? Researchers began tracking the movements of migrating birds in the late 1960s using radio telemetry , a technique that requires tagged birds to be physically followed with receiver equipment, sometimes aided by a small aircraft. Then, as GPS became more widely available in the early 2000s, satellite tags let researchers accurately track birds remotely. However, GPS transmitters are hefty — even just the battery that powers them is too heavy to be carried by the majority of small migratory songbirds, which often weigh less than a spoonful of sugar. To address this problem, researchers developed ingenious little light-level geolocators . These miniature tags minimize weight by containing only a tiny battery, clock, computer chip, and light sensor. They store data internally rather than transmitting it — hence my need to recapture tagged birds a year later. Researchers infer a bird’s locations from the timing of sunrise and sunset, which vary predictably across the globe and throughout the year. Stephanie Szarmach Each harness loop of the multisensor geolocator goes around one of the bird’s legs and the tag sits on the bird’s lower back. Light-level geolocators have opened new windows into the migrations of small birds , but they also have limitations: Their estimated locations can err by hundreds of miles, and this uncertainty becomes impractically high around the equinoxes, when day length is the same worldwide. More recently, researchers developed a newer method of geolocation that uses atmospheric pressure to circumvent these limitations. When a bird ascends during a migratory flight, a barometric geolocator records a steep drop in air pressure, capturing the timing of departure and arrival for every stop along a bird’s migration route. In between flights, the pressure the tag records reflects the elevation at the bird’s position. Knowing the bird’s elevation helps to narrow down possible locations, which researchers can then refine further by comparing the change in pressure over time recorded by the tag to global weather data using the computer program GeoPressureR . The unique pattern of rises and falls in pressure acts as a kind of pressure fingerprint for a specific location. Including light and wind data in the model of the bird’s movements can increase precision even more. Stephanie Szarmach Atmospheric pressure data collected from a multisensor geolocator carried by a yellow-rumped warbler over five days in spring. When the bird is stationary, such as when resting at a stopover site, the measured pressure remains steady. During migratory flights, when the bird ascends into the sky, the pressure drops and fluctuates dramatically. New Tech Answers an Old Question We used these new multisensor backpacks to study the migration patterns of myrtle warblers , the northern subspecies of yellow-rumped warbler, which breed across North America’s boreal forest. Myrtle warblers in the northeast are known to winter along the Atlantic and Gulf coasts, but where northwestern populations migrate has been more of a mystery. In 1899, ornithologist Richard McGregor observed myrtle warblers wintering in coastal California , and hypothesized that these birds might breed in Alaska and British Columbia. Using these new tags allowed us to test whether warblers breeding in Anchorage, Alaska, actually followed the shortest migration route to winter in California. To our surprise — and probably to McGregor’s as well, if he were still alive — we found that all the birds we tracked traveled east across the boreal forest of Canada before shifting south to the Gulf Coast – certainly not the Pacific Coast route we expected. All told, this 6,800-mile (10,900-kilometer) round-trip journey was much longer than we anticipated for a species commonly considered a short- or medium-distance migrant. Figure by Stephanie Szarmach. Warbler illustration by Emily Griffith Researchers tracked the routes six myrtle warblers flew on their fall migration southeast from Anchorage, Alaska. Why Take Such a Circuitous Route? The long, seemingly suboptimal route taken by our Alaskan myrtle warblers is actually mirrored by some other songbird species tracked from northwestern North America, including blackpoll warblers and Swainson’s thrushes . Part of this pattern may relate back to the glaciations that isolated ancient populations of birds millions of years ago. The thinking goes that as these glaciers spread, they squashed the ranges of formerly northern species into the south. Then, as the glaciers slowly receded, the forests gradually reexpanded. As more land opened up, birds moved farther north and west into that habitat. Each season some birds went a little farther as the forest available in their northern breeding grounds expanded. For migratory species such as myrtle warblers, the farther north and west their breeding range expanded, the longer the migration to their southern wintering ground became. Scientists think migration routes are genetically encoded . The birds’ genes may have traced this expansion front, like Hansel and Gretel putting down breadcrumbs as they journeyed deeper and deeper into the forest. Today’s migration routes still trace that incrementally expanded path, even though the glaciers that shaped the original boundaries are long gone. We’re still not sure exactly where the California-wintering myrtle warblers spotted in the 1800s are breeding. We suspect that a small proportion of the Anchorage-breeding birds may migrate to California , but that most of them travel from more distant, unstudied regions of Alaska or Yukon. Future research, potentially tagging myrtle warblers directly on the California wintering grounds, will shed more light on this population and why certain individuals follow a different migration route. Barometric Geolocation Provides New Data Today, this new geolocation approach improves scientists’ ability to study the migrations of small birds and supports more effective conservation actions across the course of the entire year . More precise location estimates help researchers identify key stopover and wintering sites in need of protection and better understand the threats birds face throughout their journeys. These geolocators also reveal the altitude of migratory flights, which is important for understanding the risk of birds colliding with buildings or wind turbines. Because these new tags capture pressure data for every migratory flight, they’re especially valuable for studying migration timing. Researchers have combined data from over 50 bird species to understand at what time of day or night different birds migrate . Now, as a postdoctoral researcher at the Smithsonian Migratory Bird Center , I am integrating multisensor geolocator data with satellite imagery to investigate how arrival and departure decisions throughout a bird’s migratory journey relate to seasonal changes in plant growth. Scientists have now tracked dozens of bird species with multisensor geolocators , and that number increases every year. Each mapped migratory journey improves our understanding of how small birds migrate, what factors shape their movements, and how best to protect them. items.title: Πώς οι πιστώσεις άνθρακα βοήθησαν να ξεκλειδωθεί το Εθνικό Πάρκο Great Koala στη NSW
items.titleOriginal: How carbon credits helped unlock the Great Koala National Park in NSW
items.description: ΑΠΟ ΤΗΝ ΚΑΘΗΜΕΡΙΝΗ ΣΥΝΤΑΚΤΙΚΗ ΟΜΑΔΑ OPTIMIST Το Εθνικό Πάρκο του Μεγάλου Κοάλα μπορεί να ακούγεται σαν ένα μέρος που είναι πολύ καλό για να είναι αληθινό, αλλά είναι αληθινό. Μετά από περισσότερο από μια δεκαετία προεκλογικής εκστρατείας, τρεις πολιτειακές εκλογές και πάνω από 14 ώρες κοινοβουλευτικής συζήτησης, η Νέα Νότια Ουαλία δημιούργησε το δεύτερο μεγαλύτερο εθνικό πάρκο της πολιτείας. Αποτελείται από 478.000 εκτάρια…
items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM The Great Koala National Park might sound like a place that’s too good to be true, but it is real. After more than a decade of campaigning, three state elections, and over 14 hours of parliamentary debate, New South Wales has established the state’s second-largest national park. It’s made up of 478,000 hectares (about 1.2 million acres) between Kempsey and Grafton on the Mid North Coast. More than 100 species of flora and fauna will be protected within its boundaries. The park is a patchwork of existing protected areas stitched together with more than 178,000 hectares (roughly 440,000 acres) of former state forest and Crown Land. The legislation passed through approximately 160 amendments before it got there. The campaign started small. Conservationist Ashley Love began lobbying for the park after hearing from local residents that koalas in the region weren’t as common as they once were. “It became too much to ignore,” he said. What started as a proposal to protect Crown Land eventually became a Labor election platform. NSW Labor took it to the 2015 and 2019 elections, lost both, and won government in 2023 on a ticket that included the park. Carbon credits sealed the deal Carbon credits were central to making the legislation work. The federal Clean Energy Regulator registered a project covering more than 117,000 hectares (about 289,000 acres) of the park’s state forest areas. By formally ending native forest logging there, the government can now sell carbon credits from the land. Protected forest , it turns out, generates more revenue than logged timber. Of course, that trade-off still has real costs. The Forestry Corporation of NSW had already cut more than 30 jobs in Coffs Harbour as the logging moratorium ate into forward orders. Timber NSW president Andrew Hurford laid it out: “Staff have been laid off; engineering firms that provide support to those companies have no forward orders … downstream people supplying tyres, fuel, trucking, transport, engineering. All of those things are gradually becoming slower and quieter.” The government has committed to moving displaced Forestry Corporation staff into roles with the National Parks and Wildlife Service. A park with gaps still to close NSW Environment Minister Penny Sharpe called it “a defining moment for conservation in NSW,” and by the numbers, it qualifies. Love, whose decade of advocacy made the proposal viable, was more measured. “Its nature is quite fragmented, and there are gaps and connectivity issues between sections of it, but it is a big step forward,” he said. Koalas need connected habitat to move, breed, and survive disease pressure. A 478,000-hectare patchwork is still a meaningful step up from what existed. The carbon credit structure gives the protected land a financial rationale that most past conservation campaigns lacked entirely. Love says he’ll keep pushing for the sections that didn’t make it in. After a decade, that sounds less like frustration than a habit he’s not planning to break. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . The post How carbon credits helped unlock the Great Koala National Park in NSW first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .
